Prologue to the third edition
PROLOGUE TO THE THIRD EDITION

The third edition of Saint Augustine's epistolary is now coming to light in Spanish. Since the first one appeared, the letters have already been translated into other languages, new studies have appeared and other unpublished letters have been published. That is why this third edition is presented notably corrected and enriched, corresponding to the interest that readers have gained from reading the epistolary. Authorized by the Corpus Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum Latinorum (CSEL) to publish their critical text, we offer it to our readers, also noting Migne's pagination (PL 33). We mark the pagination of both editions to facilitate comparisons and references of citations. In the Latin text we place the critical notes at the foot of the page. In the Spanish text we also place small biographical or doctrinal notes at the foot of the page. At the head of each letter we give the date, place and subject of the letter. In this way, the Latin text maintains the chronological ideal of the Maurinos, while the Spanish adjusts to the current use of vernacular translations. To balance the three volumes, we have left letters 124-140 for the second, which in the previous edition were part of the first. The third will be balanced with the new cards and indexes. The edition of the new letters, found and published by Juan Divjak (CSEL 88, year 1981), encountered serious difficulties. Inserting new letters into the collections of Migne or Goldbacher (CSEL), which adhered to the chronological order of the Maurines, would have meant sowing confusion or annulling the traditional use of citing the Augustinian epistolary. Divjak chose to edit the new letters separately in the same order as the codices he found, giving a possible chronology separately. We should do the same. These new letters will therefore appear at the end of the third volume of this edition, maintaining their own order and differentiated from the old ones by a simple asterisk.

The interest in this epistolary grows day by day. We hope, therefore, that our readers find in this third edition a source of study, spirituality and pleasure, which is undoubtedly what Saint Augustine himself expected when publishing his letters.

LETTERS AS A LITERARY GENRE

The letter is a distance communication. As such, it has been used since ancient times and in many different ways. It admits, therefore, many distinctions by its means or methods. But we actually talk about letters when it is a literary genre or communication through writing. Also in this form it admits distinctions, due to the same intention of its author or the destination of the same letter: there are public and private letters, official and reserved, literary and family letters, etc. They may also have legal meaning, either because in them an authority communicates its intention in peremptory forms, or because that authority tries to produce certain dispositions in its subjects. As such a literary genre, epistolography is framed in rhetoric. It seems that the Alexandrian rhetoricians already tried to classify the norms that were taught in schools 1. In the Roman Empire, the rhetorical models of the epistula had great influence on Latin-Christian authors, many of whom had been rhetoricians by profession. They knew the classical norms perfectly, although they had to adhere to their Christian faith. For this reason, the classical influence is more noticeable in letters of a parenetic, philosophical, ethical, social, patriotic or political type, and also when the author tries to console, edify, reprimand, order. A Christian author had to consider himself as a simple private "author", without arrogating to himself the authority of the so-called Apostolic Letters, or similar models. But these private letters frequently take on a public character, since they often deal with dogmatic doctrines, or cited biblical authorities as documentary support. Examples include those of Ambrosio, Jerónimo, Cipriano, Paulino de Ñola 2. The epistolary of Saint Augustine is of exceptional importance. At first, the saint savored the taste of language

On the other hand, the influence of Christianity on him is growing. In short, due to its personal character, it is always original. The reader will be able to verify the differential fact if he reads Agustín with Jerónimo, Paulino de Ñola, Dioscuro or Consencio. The influences that it successively receives are also noted, like a flowing river that is enriched by numerous tributaries. Such was Augustine's character: to always receive modifications and enrichments, without ever ceasing to be himself. These influences include not only Christianity, with the Bible and the Fathers before it, but also Manichaeism, skepticism, Platonism, monasticism, Donatism and social, political and private events. All this is reflected in the letters. But if these are of primary importance to know Augustine in his family and environmental intimacy, they are also important to know from within the history of the Church, at a decisive moment of its renewal and crisis, to know from within the ancient culture in its agony, to witness the birth of Europe and to see the depths of religion in general. For all this, the literary genre of letters has special strength, due to its confidential nature. Also for the external aspects of epistolography, the documentation of this epistolary is of great importance. The material used was frequently paper (papyrus) or parchment (membrana), although the most frequent and correct for family letters were waxed ivory tablets 3. The "distich", a double articulated tablet, was frequently used for short letters. This material, combined with the content of the letter, sometimes conditioned its length, distinguishing letters breviores and longiores, prolixiores and longissimae. For study letters, on doctrinal topics or for descriptions of events, there were general and special rules, and they could have unlimited length. The style is that of a direct conversation, but this also admits distinctions in formalities, content or quality of the corresponding ones. The letters were normally dictated and carried solemn treatments and formalities, as well as some form of conclusion.
They used to be sealed, as a guarantee of authenticity, when the handwriting was not known by the corresponding person in the author's signature.

The literary genre itself is somewhat vague. According to Augustine, it must bear the name of the author, the corresponding author and a theme, as opposed to "books", "treatises" and "questions" 4. However, the formalities are not always met5. Among the letters recently discovered by J. Divjak we find several "communications" (commonitoria) that could be called letters ó. Augustine himself lists some letters among his books 7. Sometimes the same materials and methods (paper, writing, copyist, collection technique per page or per line, etc.) impose on the letter, as on the treaty, the division of the parts or the ordering of the same 8. On the other hand, the style also depends on circumstances. If a certain variety can occur in all authors, in Augustine the phenomenon is very noticeable, due to time, place, circumstances, recipient, doctrinal evolution, influences, time pressure, security of the mail, copy of the writings, parallel places, etc. The strong personality of the saint has frequently served to verify the authenticity of his writings. But the fact that it has never been possible to classify the epistolary of Saint Augustine, despite having distinguished fifteen or more types of letters, proves that the literary genre should not be taken with excessive rigor.

PUBLICATION AND “COLLECTIONS”

Private letters were not intended for publication, but could accidentally be published as propaganda or as a document 27. Public letters were transmitted from hand to hand and were kept by both the authors, who kept a copy, and the correspondents, who gave them to be copied28. Augustine suggests that he expected their dissemination, and that is why he revised them 29. Such uses were common 30, but even so many letters were lost 31. The indications of Augustine himself and Possidius prove that some letters have not reached us, undoubtedly because they were not collected in traditional "collections." The mode of transmission of the epistolary is revealed by the successive and continuous appearance of new letters, evidencing that the mode of transmission was the formation of "collections" and their copying. Goldbacher believed that the collections were made over time and slowly 32. Lietzmann accepted this opinion in general, but added that Augustine had already published some small collections on particular propaganda issues; the correspondents, in turn, would have been putting together what they found at hand, and this would explain some gaps, difficult to understand 33. It is, without a doubt, the safest and most extensive source of information to know Agustín inside and out. The biographical theme suggests an important caveat. Some readers are upset when we begin to talk about a "temporary" Augustine, about Augustine's internal evolution, about the diachronic aspect of his existence. Out of an appetite for simplification and security, they would like an eternal, instantaneous, Platonic, essential Augustine, exonerated from all his individual notes, but that is impossible. It is true that we often present a character with a single photograph, or we think that in heaven each one will already have their eternal condition assured in a unique way. But that is not typical of a temporal regime, of a dispensatio temporalis, as Augustine himself says. The existence of a character offers us the existential album of all the photographs that could have been taken of him during his existence. And so, photographs will never give us the internal and dynamic process of evolution. Well, the epistolary collects this entire album of photographs, so to speak, but as testimonies and evidence of an incessant evolution. That is why the chronology of the letters is so important. The influences that Augustine receives change him internally, and, for this reason, it is necessary to know that Augustine's doctrines have a date. This does not harm either the unity or the original personality of the saint. Because unity is saved, since the influences always lead "in their own original way", and almost always with a freedom that produces amazement and strangeness. For this reason, the epistolary has great importance, since it is like a calendar of the curriculum of a career or the process and incidents of continuous progress. Nor does this oppose the different possibilities that could have existed or could have been frustrated. Peter Brown, for example, tells us about the "lost future", because the philosopher who was at his peak was ordained a priest and directed towards ecclesiastical occupations and theology. Precisely this is typical of all personalities: not knowing God's will in advance and always being prepared to change course, if necessary. When that happens, many things change meaning. Although one's own health is not usually a topic of society, sometimes we find confidences in friends36. Augustine was of a healthy constitution 37, as proven by his life of work, asceticism, concern, study, meditation, and public occupations. In the new letters this conclusion of criticism is increasingly strengthened 38. He suffers frequent ailments from his sedentary, worried life, which seem like crises of exhaustion, and which appear already in the days of his conversion, when he complains of some "lung" or "stomach" ailment, which was probably the beginning of an ulcer. He complains, then: non valeo quod voló 39. It is a paradox: he laments his lack of health to travel, and he does not stop traveling 40. To his diocesans he speaks of his infirmitas and minus ideal valeludo, as in his sermons he speaks of poor voice and lung fatigue, which, in short, seems like stress. He is grateful for being excused from traveling for lawsuits and ecclesiastical congresses 41. He also speaks of fevers similar to typhus. With old age and the cold, his ailments increased 42. In this regard, the correspondence weighs and bothers him, but when there is reason, he provokes it himself 43. That Augustine was a Manichean, a skeptic, a Platonist, does not make definitive sense except when Augustine is seen using his learning and the doctrines received and lived previously. No one will understand Augustine if he ignores that he was a rhetorician by profession. That is why Agustín's biography is the best help to know him. It has often been said that Augustine's doctrine is his own experience, his own biography.

Without entering into Augustine's philosophical system, it will be enough to remember his theories on interiority, on the a priori, etc. Augustine is frequently accused of the most opposite extremes (intellectualist, voluntarist...), and almost always due to Aristotelian prejudices. The influence of Boethius and then the predominant influence of Aristotle produces some confusion. This radical or metaphysical philosophy allows Augustine to maintain and develop his organic thought on the "true religion", unique for all men and all peoples, positive and at the same time with universal validity, illuminated and guaranteed by the hypostatic union and by supernatural, habitual and actual grace. The two aspects of human consciousness, science and wisdom, correspond to the science and wisdom of Christ. The true religion is Christ. This universalist religion is manifested above all in the fight for the unity of the Church against the Donatists and in the acceptance of the universal saving will of God, sometimes emphasizing that there are things in the Catholic Church that are not Catholic, while there are Catholic things in other religions, heresies and schisms. In this way it helps us understand the current problem of "anonymous Christians" and of Christian grace that is distributed outside the Church. It is true that this universal vision is restricted and limited by the doctrine of predestination. This doctrine is not original to Saint Augustine, but traditional, both in Manichaeism and in Christianity, and Augustine cannot help but accept it. The pressure and harassment of the Pelagians makes him sweat and bleed with unusual violence, forcing him to set boundaries and limits to his universalist thinking. But even that serves to crown his universalist vision, since he is forced to enclose himself in an impenetrable mystery. True religion is not a problem, but a mystery. A problem has a solution, current or future; a mystery is already insoluble by definition. Thus, Augustine excludes all types of naturalistic, formalist or rationalist religion, forcing man to renounce

The "true religion" or "true religion" is for Augustine a philosophical religion, and he finds a reliable witness in the epistolary. The crede ut intelligas is maintained from beginning to end, but within an evolution conditioned by theology. At first his platonic enthusiasm is strongly felt. But, after that brief period, Christian existentialism gradually took over, determined by the doctrine of original sin. Augustine settles in a dispensatio temporalis, in historical existence, in a marked temporal regime. In the epistolary we can follow the historical evolution of the saint. Predestination, grace, sin, freedom, history, the Church, are marked by that temporal and living regime of the current human regime and a history of salvation. But this acute sense of man's internal time does not make him forget the need to connect with eternity. Try, therefore, to find a concert between time and eternity, more in accordance with reality than Plato had dreamed. This ideal of Augustine already came from the time of the return of the Israelites from Babylon. The concept of "son of man" tried to solve the problem that could not be solved by the prophets, nor the Synagogue, nor the Bible, nor the angels, nor other similar types of "mediation." Christians had solved the problem by presenting Christ as God and man, that is, as a union of time with eternity. But theology had to develop those concepts. Augustine used Plato's essay to achieve those same ends, but the Neoplatonists resorted to the "mediation" of spirits, to theurgy. For Augustine, the problem was simpler, since Christ, being man and God, was in time and eternity, and united both shores like a bridge. That is why Augustine's entire doctrine was oriented towards a definitive "Christocentrism", since

"be like God." Man renounces his gigantism, his heroicism, and remains subject to the yoke of revelation through the yoke of faith. And by getting used to living in mystery, he lives subordinate (subiunctus) both in the field of science and in that of wisdom, which occur together in Christ.
THE THEOLOGY OF UNITY

If Piustino had accentuated in Augustine a "mystique of unity", Christianity illuminated that mystique: "We discussed where the Church is... Without a doubt it is unique and our elders called it Catholic" 47. "Whatever truth you find, retain it and attribute it to the Catholic Church; "Whatever falsehoods you find, reject them and forgive me, who am a man" 48. The Church is, therefore, unique, universal, by representing Christ, who is unique and universal. For this concept of "universal religion" it is not necessary that all men or peoples agree in fact, but rather a universality of law is sufficient, and Augustine insists that the Church receives all humanity, Christian or non-Christian, heretics, schismatics, sinners, etc., each one according to his situation. And just as Christ does not manifest himself in his divinity, but in his humanity, in temporal kenosis, so also the Church manifests herself in time, not in eternity, and that is why it is said: "Christianity is not a finished religion, but only the path that leads to it. It is not the end, but the only stage. It is an interim, full of tension and struggle, darkness and risk, but also of certain faith and joyful hope. That is why it corresponds to a bold faith: the victory that has overcome the world is our faith (1 Jn 5,4)» 49. It is the formula that struck Newmann when he read in an article by Wiseman the Augustinian sentence: securus iudicat orbis terrarum, bonds non esse qui se dividunt ab orbe terrarum in quacumque parte terrarum. The entire reality of the Church, together visible and invisible, like Christ, presupposes a law that we could call "the law of the redemptive incarnation", the invisible presence of the Spirit of Christ, that is, "the mystical principle of unity." This dynamic principle comes from the Father through the mission of the Son and the Spirit, and returns to the Father through the impulse or love of the Es47

spirit and the living presence of Christ in habitual and actual grace. This principle of unity, which is the love of the Spirit and the presence of the grace of Christ, is, at the same time, immanent and transient, it is the "energy of form" and at the same time the gift of God. For this reason, the Church, the true religion, is not a human construction, but a new divine creation in time, a divine regime imposed on man in his situation as a sinner. That is why Augustinian thought not only surpasses all philosophy, but also all theology, so to speak, to penetrate a mystical terrain, a systematic mysticism of unity. The formula "unity through charity" is nothing other than the action of the spirit of Christ, of the mission of the Spirit, or of Love. That transcendent and immanent Love unifies all men, all the faithful, in a single organism, in a mystical Body. No one ignores the difficulties, today insurmountable, that this Church, the mystical Body of Christ, encounters in achieving its historical unity on earth. We have inherited a very different history and culture from that environment in which Augustine moved within the African Church. And yet, many of its principles can serve as a guide for us to maintain hope, since we will never know what the future of the Church will be like. And, on the other hand, the "mystique of unity" is a principle of universal value that can keep alive our faith and our hope in the ways of God. Neither Augustine's theory nor praxis on Donatism could be strictly applied today to the separate confessions of the Catholic Church. And yet, Cardinal Newman, who considered the aggregation of the Anglican Church to the Catholic Church impossible, had to recognize the Augustinian formula: securus iudicat orbis terrarum! 9.

The epistolary style allows for greater vivacity and temperamental and personal influence. And if this tendency was already noticeable in all African writers, it could not be missing in Augustine in any of his writings, but especially in his letters. From the beginning of his priesthood he intervened passionately in the Donatist controversy 50. Many positions, apparently dubious, are better understood from the epistolary, taking into account 50 Letters 23 and 33.

of the circumstances. Thus Augustine can serve as a model for current apologetics due to his constructive firmness and, at the same time, his charity and understanding. Especially if we take into account the adaptation to different characters, places and times, and to the different positions adopted by heretics, schismatics, Catholics, men and women of different conditions. It is highly instructive to follow the chronological order of the letters to understand the internal and external process of the controversies, the period of trials and that of definitive conclusions. Donatism, for example, seems at first to be a matter of clerical abuse and fanaticism, but it soon appears as a radical denial of the Christian spirit, a doctrinal, racial, social revolution, with a strictly religious root. The same thing happens with Pelagianism, which at first appears as a demand for moral and humanistic perfection, a psychological complex of superiority, a heroicism, and then shows its deep and distant roots. We often get bogged down in doctrinal problems as if they were the entirety of a problem, and we forget the revolutionary movement of the real human problem. Only in this way do we understand why Donatism or Pelagianism compromises Augustine's religion in its entirety, and we understand why Augustine takes so heartily and with such passion such a combat in which his own existence and his entire mentality are at stake. We then see the need for an Augustinian Christocentrism, not as an abstract discussion or as a pious dialectic or rhetoric, but as a universal theory of religion, as a "philosophical religion", as the only true religion 51. Augustine combats all heresies, schisms, deviations and revolutions from the same point of view, which is his own "true religion." God has to enter human history through the incarnation: only in this way does the Word of God, made flesh, enter humanity. This has no way to God except in Jesus Christ; and God has his way to man in Jesus Christ. Christ as man is a positive religion; but as a Word it provides a participation in universal truth and value: there is, therefore, outside of this "God-man" a true religion. 51 Letters 33,140, ​​etc.

Agustín is a very argumentative man. Almost all complaints of human freedom are turned against him. It is not only the Pelagians, Marxists, libertines, pluralists, humanists and revolutionaries who accuse him. The same conservative Catholics denounce him. The best remedy against such denunciations and accusations is to read this epistolary and face it with an ardent and open heart, although within the limitations of his time, which are never or almost never properly due to him. It is common to praise the genius and authority of Augustine, to level accusations against him that we do not dare to address to Saint Paul, to the Church or to God. Instead of considering the saint as the victim of an inexorable tradition, we put all our sins on him, as on the victim of sacrifice. It is curious this phenomenon that is observed so frequently today. Augustine was a Manichaean, an idealist of "perfection", who, upon converting, wanted to be a "perfect Christian", not a "semi-Christian", as the Manichaeans used to say. In this concept he became a "reformer" at the service of the Church, willing to fight and polemic against his enemies from within and without. Guided by that spirit, he had to combine it with boundless kindness, with cordial kindness. Those who accuse him of being a rigorist and a Manichean forget that both the Manicheans and the Donatists and Pelagians were rigorist movements, which exaggerated man's strength to burden him with excessive responsibilities, and that Augustine denounced all these displays of "humanism" precisely to praise human weakness and make the yoke of the Lord bearable. He was always a defender of human freedom, which he never renounced, for which he fought exaggeratedly when he discovered the possible conflict with effective grace and which he covered with the veils of mystery so that no one could compromise it. The epistolary is the best testimony of his reformist desire. From the beginning he rejected ascetic "heroicism" and humanistic gigantism, leaning more towards Alexandria than towards Antioch, towards love rather than towards human justice. From the beginning he eliminated penitence contests, demonstrations and displays of resistance, and sporting marks of continence, giving more importance to "intention" than to "objective morality", although respecting the rights of the latter. His S.Ag. 8

Asceticism was always moderate, cultured, spiritual, focused on charity and unity. The difference between objective and subjective morality has been studied a lot in Augustine, but today it is more interesting than ever. Another reason for objection is the supposed "idealism." On the contrary, the dispensatio temporalis, which Augustine takes from the Bible, presents a sensible world, permeated by intelligibility, in which the so-called "Franciscan mysticism" spontaneously flourishes. We can conclude that there is no letter that is not interesting to better understand the heart of Augustine.

in the theological and mystical vision of the mature and experienced Augustine 54. Although the entire epistolary reflects the monastic spirit of Augustine and his religious intentions, there are a good number of letters that help to closely and vividly understand his monastic ideals, necessary to understand Augustine himself 55.

Augustine is a monk, that is, in his opinion, a perfect Christian. But he placed monasticism at the public service of the Church, giving it a triple function: 1) penetration into the popular masses, who came from paganism and joined the Church with its defects; 2) apologetic struggle against Manichaeism and then against any external enemy of the Church itself; 3) ascetic struggle against ecclesiastical abuses. He did not "monasticize" the Church, but rather "ecclesiastize" monasticism. It did not convert the monk into a rank in the hierarchy, but it did convert him into a very useful, or perhaps essential, piece of ecclesiastical life. The monk can be a layman, a clergyman, a canon or a bishop, without losing his own character. The Donatists immediately realized Augustine's intention and denounced him as the inventor of a way of life whose effectiveness against them was manifest 52. As soon as the saint arrived in Africa, he began his monastic work in Tagaste, in his paternal house 53, and converted the monastery into an academy for training fighters. By organizing the monastery of Hippo, he essentially expanded his vision, helped by reading the Bible, and especially the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 2:4), which provided him with a "theology of Pentecost." This new vision of monasticism increased with the study of Saint Paul and with the decisive influence of the theories of original sin, predestination and gratia Christi, when the anti-Pelagian struggle began. Although in recent times studies on monasticism have multiplied, we still need studies that situate this monasticism. Cf. Reply to the letters of Petilian III 40,48. The epistolary with Nebridio for the early days of Tagaste is interesting. Letters 22, 2 and 4.

Two notes, which seem opposite, are strongly evident in Augustine's epistolary style: on the one hand, his strong and unmistakable personality, and on the other, the variety of styles or capacity for adaptation. Agustín's style has an air of endearing intimacy, of human and friendly warmth. The African soul that recreates itself in the bombastic, inciting, sharp, picturesque dialectic, with a tendency toward irony and ad hominem argument, has its typical representative in Augustine, although marked by the personality of the author. Almost all letters can serve as a model, even in those situations or occasions that have no parallel in other authors. It is difficult to find another writer in whom the warm, frank and direct meaning that Augustine uses with his friends and enemies, with heretics, schismatics, sinners, proud, stubborn, unscrupulous, men and women, is so delicately pointed out. Sometimes it even makes us doubt those flattering and excessively affectionate formulas. He respects all official treatments and customs, but his personal position soon becomes apparent. Rhetorical norms, if they existed, are left aside. The ecclesiastical condition gives this human warmth a certain religious and restrained meaning. For all these reasons, the style itself has frequently served as a criterion for judging the authenticity of some letters. At the same time we see that, although there is no concern for style, there is a wonderful adaptation to personal and real circumstances. The style often depends on the corresponding or the character and content of the letter. Sometimes, the saint shows off literary preparation, periods, rhythm, chains of clauses, syntax, use and abuse of conjunctions, use of treatments and legal rules. By The meaning of monasticism varies and evolves with Augustine himself, although the fundamental lines of monasticism itself are maintained. That is why so many opinions and discussions have arisen about the so-called "founding charisma" of Augustinian monasticism. Especially interesting are the letters exchanged with Nebridius, Valerio, Aurelius, Alypius, Eudoxius and Paulinus of Ñola.

In general, everything depends on the degree of friendship or enmity, the status of the corresponding civil or ecclesiastical hierarchy, orthodoxy or heterodoxy, theme, sex, etc. We would say that there are different styles, judging by the variety of models. It seems obvious to us that official or business letters have their own formulas. It also seems obvious to us that in many cases we find parallel places with other books that were dictated at the same time and with the same haste. Finally, it seems obvious to us that the letters reflect the evolution of the author's thinking and the circumstances of a debate. But we are always left with the same and different Augustine, capable of always being himself and adopting the appropriate figure in each case. The generic nature of the literary genre, distance conversation, allows for all kinds of combinations and witticisms.

And it is about Augustine himself and the historical and critical period in which he lived. North African scholars who do not scrutinize this epistolary naively believe that the Donatist conflict seems like a class struggle or European colonialism. RELEVANCE OF THE EPISTOLARY

With what has been said we have enough to realize the importance of this epistolary. Without a doubt, its greatest interest lies in doctrinal issues, in controversies and apologetic methods, and in the points that we have already mentioned. But it doesn't just reside there. To appreciate this importance we collect the note that Fr. Goulven Madec took from the round table on the new letters published by Divjak, held on September 20 and 21, 1982. «The contribution (of those letters) to the historical geography of Roman Africa (MM. Dessauges and Lancel), to the practices of selling children (M. Humbert), to colonialism and slavery (M. Lapelley), to swindling and banditry was highlighted. (M. Rouge); Bonner, Bouhot and Wermelinger), to the Donatist controversy (M. Schindler) and a note of Augustine's activities from September 11 to December 1, 418 (P. Berrouard)». We are dealing here with only a handful of letters that, because they lacked high doctrinal value, were little copied and went unnoticed until now, but which contained extraordinary importance.

Master Juan de Amerbach made the first edition in Basel, in 1943. He used a codex from the Monacense family. It contained only 183 cards. Erasmus republished them as the second volume of his Opera Augustini (Basel 1528) in the printing press of Juan Froben. He made literary corrections. The same printing press re-edited the epistolary in 1569, adding 38 new letters, including 16 from the Parisiense codex and another 16 offered by Martin of Lipsia. The Leuven edition (Antverpia 1576) appeared corrected and augmented with another 29 letters. In 1654-1655 Jerome Vignier published the supplement to all the works of Saint Augustine published before 1614, in two volumes. The first of them contained 65 letters, which had been published as new by the second edition of Froben and that of the Louvanians. Lucas Reinhart made a separate edition of the epistolary (Frankfurt 1668). The Maurinos prepared the monumental edition, adding 16 new letters and, for the first time, the 29th (Paris 16791700). Migne collected this edition in volume 33 of his Latin Patrology, with the addition of 2 new letters. Finally, Goldbacher presented the critical edition (vol.34, 44,57 and 58 of the Corpus Scriptorum Ecclesiastkorum latinorum). Makes the classification and evaluation of the codices, noting in

each letter those that contain it. Critics have pointed out some defects in this edition, either because some cards have few representatives and it is not easy to apply a criterion, or because, sometimes, Goldbacher's criteria are not convincing. But, despite everything, this critical edition is the best we know. In addition to those contained in Migne, he included two new letters and a fragment of a third, which he included within Migne's numbering, namely: 92 A; 173 A; 185 A. It also included, out of numbering, a letter published for the first time by C. Morin in "Revue Bénédictine" 18 (1901) 241-244, which in the present edition will be numbered 212 A. After Goldbacher's edition, C. Lambot published a new one in "Revue Bénédictine" 51 (1939) 109-121, which It will be numbered 212 A. Finally, in 1981, the edition of 27 new letters appears by Juan Divjak, who discovered them (CSEL 88).

Listen, then, more carefully to what this means in my favor. Some criticize that very noble Socratic theory in which it is stated that the things we learn are not instilled in us as novelties, but rather that they are brought to memory through recollection. They allege that memory refers to past things, while the things we see with intelligence, as Plato himself affirms, always remain and cannot perish, and, therefore, are not past. But they do not notice that this vision is past, since we have already seen such things with our minds. When we separate ourselves from them and begin to see other things, we see them again through reminiscence, that is, through memory. Therefore, omitting other things, eternity always remains and has no need for imaginary fictions that serve as vehicles to bring it to mind, although it could not come if we did not remember it. 36. Well, what comes from why we imagine what we do not see? What do you think except that there is infused in the soul a singular power to decrease and increase, and that it necessarily carries it with it wherever it goes? Such power can be discovered primarily in numbers. Because of it it happens that, for example, when the image of a crow is presented to our gaze, which was already known by sight, by adding and subtracting details we arrive at a certain image never seen before. Thus it happens that in spirits accustomed to moving between such fictions, these figures slip into thought as if spontaneously. And so, when a soul imagines, it can, through those details that the sense introduced, subtracting and adding, as I have said, generate images that it did not perceive in their entirety by any sense, although it had perceived all those details in one thing or another. We, boys born and raised next to the Mediterranean, just by seeing the water in a small glass, we could already imagine the sea, while the taste of strawberries and durillos did not come to mind before tasting them in Italy. This is why people born blind do not know what to answer when asked about light and colors: they have not received colored images, since they have not felt any. 7. Date: Year 390/391. Place: Tagaste. Topic: Sending books and invitation to perseverance. AUGUSTINE TO GAYO

I cannot express to you the emotion that your memory produced and continues to produce in me, as soon as I left you. Because I remembered that the modesty of your discussion was not altered by your admirable desire to investigate. I have hardly found a person, neither more courageous to ask nor more calm to listen. That's why I would have liked to talk to you more; It would never be much, no matter how long the time spent, when it comes to you. But that is difficult and why are we going to enumerate the causes? It is difficult in fact, although perhaps one day it will be very easy. God willing, but now it's difficult. That is why I commissioned a brother, through whom I am sending you this letter, to give your most prudent charity all my writings to read. I won't have to force you to read me, because I know how much kindness you harbor in your spirit towards me. If you approve of what you read and perceive that it is true, do not think that it is mine, except as it has been granted to me. 1. Both of us, Alipio and I, owe you an answer. But you will receive one of the two parts recharged, since you see Alypius present there, by whose words you will welcome me. I ask above all that your religious prudence thinks that in this life, especially in these times, there is nothing easier, more pleasant and more accepted among men than the ministry of bishop, priest or deacon, if it is carried out for mere compliance and adulation. These rites were not condemned, but were replaced by others more appropriate to the time. For just as the first coming of the Lord abolished circumcision, so the second coming will abolish baptism. It brings us such a great radiance of your charity that it seemed to us, not only to know, but to recognize your charity. Because this charity comes from him who predestined us for himself from the beginning of the world. In Him we were made before we were born, since He made us and we were not made, for He makes the things that will be. By his foreknowledge and activity we were formed in likeness of wills and unity of faith or faith of unity. We are united by a charity that anticipates the news, so that we already know each other in spirit, by the spirit that reciprocally reveals to us, even before we physically see each other. Therefore we congratulate and glorify in the Lord, who, being always one and the same, produces his charity everywhere in his people through the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out on all flesh, rejoicing his city with the impetus of that torrent; among whose citizens he has deservedly placed you, prince among the princes of his people, in an apostolic see. And he also wanted to count us, fallen, in your lot, those whom he raised up; miserable ones whom he brought out of the dust. But we rejoice more in that mercy of the Lord, by which he has lodged us in the sanctuary of your heart. In fact, we have received the distinguished and main work of your love and concern, the work of the holy and perfect man in Christ the Lord, our brother Augustine, composed of five books: we admire it and receive it in such a way that its words seem to us dictated by heaven. Encouraged by that confidence that the coincidence of feelings gives us, we have ventured to write to him; You will excuse us to him for our incompetence and recommend us to his charity. Also recommend to us all those saints, whose benevolence, even though they were far away, you have transmitted to us. Take the same interest in offering them our greetings through you, considering us as companions in the clergy of your holiness and as emulators of your faith and virtue in the monasteries. Date: Around 394. Place: Ñola. Topic: Commendation of Augustine's books and request from others. PAULINO and THERASIA,
sinners, to AUGUSTINE, venerable lord and brother and of one soul with us.

1. This charity of Christ that spurs us on and brings together those who are absent in the unity of faith has made us abandon our reservations and given us the confidence to write to you. In my bowels you have been impressed by those letters of yours that, springing from the scholastic faculties and sweetened in the honeycombs of heaven, I have gathered as medicine and food for the soul in five books. I received them as a gift from the blessed and venerating bishop of our Alypius, not only for our instruction, but also for the usefulness of many cities within the Church. I now read these books: in them I find my delights and that food that does not perish, but produces the substance of eternal life, through that faith that incorporates us into Jesus Christ our Lord. Our faith is strengthened by the writings and examples of the faithful, since it disdains the visible and longs for the invisible, thanks to the charity that believes everything, according to the truth of omnipotent God. Furthermore, I did not receive your letter by a courier that could carry mine. Well, what you want me to ask of you, I have asked in a letter with the clarity that I have deemed appropriate; You will see if I have achieved it. If, however, I do not succeed, when I find out or when you remind me again, I will do better. Until now our conversations were perhaps like a rumor of the chains of this life; Listen now briefly to my heartiest concerns and longings about your enduring hope. Maybe there will be some way to open your way to God. 2. My Licencio: I fear that you will become harmfully and viciously involved in perishable businesses, for refusing and fearing so much the bonds of wisdom. Because wisdom comes forward to pressure her own, she trains them with certain exercises and fatigue, but she finally lets them go and surrenders to their embrace when they are free. Those whom he first educates with temporary bonds, he then imprisons with eternal bonds. No sweeter or closer bond can be imagined. I confess that the first part of that education is somewhat severe, but I will not say that the second is harsh, since it is so sweet; It is not springy either, since it is so vigorous. I believe that it is deleterious to believe that the Holy Books contain any lies, that is, that those authors through whom the Scripture was given to us have told any lies in their books. It is one thing to wonder if a good man can lie in some circumstances, and quite another thing to wonder if a writer of Holy Scripture could lie. Better said, it is not another question, but rather there is no question. Because, once a lie is admitted due to the demands of the apostolic office in such a high summit of authority, no particle of the Books will be defended. By the same deleterious rule, the intention and obligation of the ministry of the lying author can always be resorted to, according to each person's whim, when a passage is difficult for customs or incredible for faith. 4. 5. I returned the Exodus codex and unmasked, as time permitted, the sin of drunkenness. I opened the letters of Saint Paul and noted among which sins he mentioned it, reading that passage: if any brother is condemned as a fornicator, idolater, covetous, curser, drunkard or thief, do not eat anything with him. I explained to them, moaning, how dangerous there is in participating in the table of those who get drunk at home. Next I read what is said not far from the previous passage: Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor effeminates, nor sodomites, nor thieves, nor the covetous, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor thieves, will possess the kingdom of God. And of these you were, but you were washed and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God. After this reading, I asked them with what face they could hear that you have been washed by those who maintain such impure lust in their hearts, that is, in the inner temple of God, since the kingdom is closed to it. Then I went on to that other chapter that says: When you come together, it is no longer to celebrate the Lord's Supper, since each one takes his own beforehand to consume it; one goes hungry, and another gets drunk. Do you have no houses to eat and drink, or do you despise the church of God? Having recited the passage, I warned that in the church one should not celebrate or even con-

honest and sober vites. The Apostle did not say: "Do you not have houses to get drunk?", as if drunkenness were the only thing that is prohibited within the church. He said to eat and drink, and those who have houses where they can nourish themselves with appropriate food can honestly do that; but they must always do it outside the church. And yet, in the anguish of these troubled times and lost customs, we had reached such a point that we could wish for certain Christians, not only moderate feasts, but even the kingdom of debauchery, as long as they became drunk within their homes. 6. I quoted the chapter of the Gospel that I had expounded the day before, and it deals with the pseudo-prophets, saying: by their fruits you will know them. I forced them to consider how shameful and lamentable it was that they not only lived on the fruits of the flesh privately, but that they wished to take away its honor from the church, and fill the entire wide space of this great basilica with mobs of gluttons and drunkards, with a supposed authorization. Once all this was finished, I returned the codex and with all earnestness I ordered them to pray, prey to the anguish to which the danger reduced me, with all the strength that the Lord deigned to instill in me. I presented the common danger to everyone, that of them who had been entrusted to my care and mine, since I had to give an account of all to the Prince of Shepherds, for whose humility, great affronts, slaps, spitting in the face, slaps, crown of thorns, cross and blood, I begged them that, if they themselves had failed in something, they would take pity on me. I reminded them of the ineffable charity that the venerable old man Valerius professed to me; He did not hesitate to impose on me the dangerous obligation of exposing the word of Truth, and he frequently repeated to them that their prayers had been heard with my coming, celebrating that I did not come to die with

them nor to contemplate their death, but to fight with them to achieve eternal life together. Finally, I warned them that I was trusting and resting in him who does not know how to lie and made the promise through the mouth of the prophet, referring to our Lord Jesus Christ: If your children abandon my law and do not walk in my precepts; If they profane my provisions, I will visit their crimes with the rod and their crimes with the scourge; but I will not withhold my mercy from them. I told them, then, that if they despised the warnings that I had warned them and read, I trusted in God that he would visit them with the rod and the whip and would not allow them to be condemned to this world. In this complaint of mine I acted according to the encouragement and ingenuity that our Tutor and Governor instilled in me, in accordance with the magnitude of the danger. It was not my tears that caused theirs, for I confess that, while I was speaking, they came forward to cry and I could not restrain myself from doing the same. After crying together, I ended my talk with full hope of correction. 8. Date: Year 395. Place: Ñola. Theme: Recommendation and Poem by Licencio. PAULINO yTERASIAa ROMANIANO, just and praiseworthy lord and ho-

noble brother. 1. The day before delivering this letter to the mail, our brothers arrived back from Africa, whose lateness had us nervous, as you saw, oh you, the most desired of all the holy and dear men. With them we received different letters, namely from Aurelius, Alypius, Augustine, Profuturus and Severus, all of whom are now bishops. Enthusiastic, then, with the responses of such and such holy men, we have hastened to express our joy to you to make you participate with these joyful indications of the joy that is expected in that journey that concerns us. If you already know this, because other ships have brought you news of those venerable and beloved men, please accept this repetition and rejoice again with renewed pleasure. If we are the first to tell you the news, celebrate that in your country we have been offered so much charity, by the grace of Christ; Either we are the first or we are among the first to know what divine Providence is doing there, always admirable in its saints, as it is written. 2. We write this not only to celebrate that Augustine has received the episcopacy, but also that the Churches of Africa have deserved from God that favor of receiving the heavenly word from the mouth of Augustine. For the greater glory of the divine office he has been called in a new way: he has been consecrated, not to succeed, but to accompany the bishop in the chair. Thus Augustine is auxiliary bishop of the church of Hippo, while Valerius is healthy. The blessed old man, on whose most pure spirit a stain of livid envy has never fallen, now collects from the Most High the fruits that he has deserved with the peace of his heart; Thus, whom he wished to have simply as a successor to his pontificate, he deserved to have him as a colleague. Could this have been believed before it happened? Also in this Providence of the Omnipotent, that of the Gospel could be repeated: For men this is arduous; but with God everything is possible. Let us rejoice, then; Let us rejoice in Him who is unique in doing wonders, who makes the brothers live together in one house, because he looked at our humility and visited his people with good; He raised it with his power in the house of David his servant and now he has strengthened it with the power of his Church in these select ones of his, to suppress the power of sinners, that is, of the Donatists and Manichaeans, as promised by the prophet. 3. 4. (Letter addressed to Licentius.) Listen, then, son, to the law of your father, that is, the faith of Augustine, and do not reject the advice of your mother, a sweet name that also rightly claims the piety of Augustine. When you were little, he carried you in his womb, fed you with the first milk of secular wisdom, and now he wants to breastfeed you and nourish you also in the Lord with a spiritual breast. Although you are already an adult by bodily age, in the spiritual realm he sees you still babbling in the cradle, still without the speech of the word of God, dragging yourself in Christ with the first steps and faltering legs: may the doctrine of Augustine, like the hand of a mother or a nurse, be able to support the little hesitating child. If you listen to him and follow, I will once again encourage you with the words of Solomon: Son, you will receive on your head a crown of graces. And then you will be, not that pontiff and consul dreamed of in the imagination, but one formed by Truth itself: Christ will be in charge of filling with the effects of his solid operation the hollow fantasies of a false enterprise. You will truly be pontiff and consul, O Lycentius!, if, following the prophetic vestiges and the apostolic disciplines of Augustine, you join yourself to him, as the blessed Elyseus joined the holy Elijah, or the adolescent Timothy joined the illustrious Apostle. Without separating yourself from him on the divine route, so that you learn to deserve the priesthood with a perfect heart and to direct the people towards salvation with the word of a teacher. 5. Paulinus and Terasia to Romaniono

With few words and insistence, my Licentius, you can be enthusiastic about Christ, since since childhood you have been inflamed by the spirit and words of the venerable Augustine towards the search for truth and wisdom, which are both found in Christ, the highest good of all good. And if he achieved little fruit from you and for you, what will I achieve, who arrived so late and lack his abundance? But, confident in the effectiveness of his action and in the goodness of your ingenuity, and thinking that you already possess better and greater assets than those you still lack, I have dared to speak for a double reason: to compare myself with that great man in his concern for you and to count myself, due to my accredited affection, among those who love your health. I know well that regarding the influence on your perfection, the floor must be given to Augustine. I fear, son, that I have offended your ear with the harshness of my reckless words and that I have caused the wound of my boredom in your spirit. But your poem comes to mind, through which I saw that you are familiar with musical modes: I was fond of that desire at your age. to PROCULEYANO, honorable and beloved sir.

1. For fear of the ineptitude of the inexperienced, I no longer have to explain the title of my letter to you. We try to convince each other of error, and many will not know which of us is wrong until there is full discussion of the cause. But we will both render each other a service if we act with good intentions to liquidate this calamity of discord. Although most men do not see it, God, for whom the heart has no doors, sees the sincerity and the trembling of Christian humility with which mine works. On the other hand, you will easily understand what it is that I want to honor in you: I do not consider worthy of any honor the error of schism, from which I wish to cure all men, as far as I am on my side. I want, without doubts or hesitation, to honor you, because you are united to me with the bonds of human society and because in you signs of a placid soul are discovered; Therefore, I hope that you will easily embrace the truth once you see it XXXIII [CSEL 34/2,18]
