Rogo te atque obsecro, si est in te aliqua humanitas, quam multi praedicant, hic appareat bonitos tua, si non propter honores transitionos simulatur, ut contremescant in te uiscera misericordiae et uelis aliquando rem discutí urging nobiscum orationibus et omnia pacifice conferendo, ne miserae plebes, quae nostris honoribus obsequuntur, premant nos obsequiis suis in iudicio dei, sed potius nostra non ficta [23] caritate nobiscum reuocatae ab erroribus et dissensionibus in ueritatis et pacis itinera dirigantur. I opto te coram oculis dei beatum esse, domine honorabilis et dilectissime. "For your crown!" This formula, which was applied to martyrs and confessors, was maintained among monks, above all. Saint Jerome applies it to Saint Augustine.

Date: Year 396. Place: Hippo. Topic: Donatist controversy. AUGUSTINE to EUSEBIO, distinguished lord and worthy of welcome and honorable brother. 1. God, to whom the arcana of the human heart are patent, knows that the more I love Christian peace, the more I am moved by the sacrilegious exploits of those who unworthily and perversely persevere in schism. But that commotion of my spirit is peaceful; I am not trying to ensure that no one is forced by force to enter the Catholic communion, but that the evident truth be made evident to all who err, so that, through my ministry and with the help of God, the same manifest truth can be embraced and followed. 2. Please, is there anything more execrable than what happened recently, to keep quiet? A young man who, insane, repeatedly hits his mother, who does not remove his impious hands from the wombs that gave him life, is corrected by his bishop, not even in those days when the severity of the laws forgives even the greatest criminals. He threatens to join Donato's party and finish her off in that incredible frenzy with which he usually hits her. After amenaXXXIV [CSEL 34/2,23]
DOMINO EXIMIO MERITOQUE SUSCIPIENDO ATQUE HONORABILI FRATRI EÜSEBIO AUGUSTINUS

1. Scit deus, cui manifesta sunt arcana cordis humani, quantum pacem diligo Christianam, tantum me moueri sacrilegis eorum factis, qui in eius dissensione indigne atque impie perseuerant, eumque motum animi mei esse pacificum ñeque me id agere, ut ad communionem catholicam quisquam cogatur inuitus, sed ut omnibus errantibus aperta ueritas declaretur et per nostrum ministerium deo iuuante manifestata se amplectendam atque sectandam satis ipsa persuadeat. 2. Quid enim execrabilius, quaeso te, ut alia taceam, quam id, quod nunc accidit? corripitur ab episcopo suo iuuenis crebris caedibus matris insanus et impías manus nec illis diebus, cum etiam seueritas legum sceleratissimis parcit, a [24] uisceribus, unde natus est, reuocans; minatur eidem matri se in partem Donati translaturum et eam, quam incredibili furore solet caedere, perempturum; minatur ei, transit ad partem

Zarla, he goes over to the Donatist party, he is baptized in his fury, he is clothed in the white garment of the neophyte, while he rages in the blood of his mother. He is placed in an eminent and prominent place within the enclosure, he is presented as renewed in the eyes of all the faithful who groan, that man who is plotting matricide. 3. Do you like all this, very serious man? I would never believe it about you, because I know your sanity. The carnal mother is beaten in the members that engendered and nourished the ungrateful. The Church, spiritual mother, forbids it. She is also beaten in the sacraments with which she engendered and nourished the ungrateful. Doesn't it seem to you as if the parricide had bellowed: "What will I do to the Church, which forbids me from mistreating my mother?" I already know what I have to do. I am going to hurt her with the blows that she can receive: I will execute something on me that will make her limbs ache. I will go over to those who know how to expel from me the grace, by which I was born there, and destroy the life that I received in their wombs; I will torture both my mothers with cruel torments; The one who gave me the light the last will be the first to suffer. With their pain I will die spiritually, with their wounds I will live carnally. What can we expect, oh Eusebius, honorable man? They will provide weapons to this new Donatist against a poor woman, old, decrepit, destitute of vigor, whose bad treatment the Catholic Church prohibited. What else did he conceive in his furious heart Donati, rebaptizatur furens et in maternum sanguinem fremens albis uestibus candidatur; I constituted tur intra cancellos eminens atque conspicuus et omnium gemmentium oculis matricidii meditator tamquam renouatus opponitur. 3.

Haecine tandem tibí placent, uir grauissime? nequaquam hoc de te crediderim; noui considerationem tuam. caeditur mater carnalis in membris, quibus genuit et nutriuit ingratum; prohibet hoc ecclesia, mater spiritalis; caeditur et ipsa in sacramentis, quibus genuit et nutriuit ingratum. nonne tibi uidetur dixisse parricidaliter frendens: «Quid faciam ecclesiae, quae me prohibet caedere matrem meam? inueni, quid faciam: iniuriis, quibus potest, etiam ipsa fairtur; fiat in me aliquid, unde membra eius doleant; uadam mihi ad eos, qui nouerunt exsufflare gratiam, in qua ibi a natus sum, destrure formam, quam in uterus eius accepi; both matres meas saeuis cruciatibus torqueam; quae me posterior peperit, efferat prior; ad huius dolorem spiritaliter moriar, ad illius caedem carnaliter uiuam. quid aliud expectamus, uir honorabilis Eusebi, nisi ut in miseram mulierem senectute decrepitam, uiduitate destitutam, a cuius caedibus in catholica prohibebatur, iam Donatista securus armetur? quid enim aliud furibundo corde concepit, cum diceret a]

by saying to his mother: "I will join Donato's party and drink your blood"? Already bloodied, his conscience has dressed in white; He has already executed half of his promise; The second part is missing: drinking his mother's blood. If this may please you, let your clerics and sanctifiers encourage you to fully fulfill your promise within the octave. 4. Powerful is the right hand of the Lord to turn away the fury of a wicked man from that sad and desolate widow, to terrify him with the ways that He knows and force him to abandon such a criminal disposition. But what should I do, shaken by such pain, but at least speak? They behave like this, and they tell me: "Shut up!" God save me from such madness, because He commanded by His Apostle and ordered the bishop to refute those who teach what is not appropriate. The horror of your indignations will not silence me. I have already recorded this horrendous crime in a public record, so that, while I deplore it, no one can imagine that I invented it. I did it thinking above all of other cities where there was room. Isn't it already said in Hippo itself that Proculeianus did not order what the public record denounces? 5. Is there any greater modesty in me than to discuss this serious matter with you, since you are endowed with a very clear dignity and such reflective sanity? I begged you, through the good brothers and honest men that I sent to your eminent

cia, what I ask of you now: deign to inform me if Victor, the presbyter of Proculeiano, did not receive from his bishop that mandate that the public records proclaim. Perhaps Victor ambiguously said something else and the records attribute it to Proculeiano, because he was from the same communion. If Proculeyan admits the charge, I agree that we can placidly deal with the whole matter of our dissent, so that the error, which is already manifest, may become even more evident. I have heard that Proculeiano proposed a deal to see where the truth is, according to the Scriptures, without popular noise, in the presence of ten serious men from both sides. It is completely ridiculous what some have brought to my ears as a Proculeian proposition: that I should have gone to Constantine, when so many Donatist bishops gathered there, or that I should go to Milevi, because there, as it says, they are going to have a council shortly. I have no other mission of my own than to care for the church of Hippo. I have to discuss the entire reason for this dispute with Proculeiano. Now, if he finds himself incapable of arguing, ask for help from any of his colleagues. When it comes to the Church, I do not enter other cities except with the permission or request of the bishops of those cities, my brothers and priests. 6. I don't quite understand how Proculeiano, who has called himself a bishop for so many years, should be afraid of me, a novice, when it comes to arguing. What does it have to do with here

matri: «Transferam me [25] in partem Donati et bibam sanguinem (133) tuum»? ecce iam conscientia cruentus, ueste dealbatus perficit partem pollicitationis suae; restat pars altera, ut matris sanguinem bibat. si etgo placent ista, urgeatur a clericis et sanctificatoribus suis, ut intra octauas suas totum, quod uouit, exoluat. 4. Potens est quidem dextera domini, quae furorem illius a misera uidua et desolata compescat et eum, quibus modis nouit, a tam scelerata dispositione deterreat. uerum tamen ego Tanto animi dolore percussus quid facerem, nisi saltem loquerer? an uero ist illi faciunt et mihi dicitur: Tace? auertat a me dominus hanc amentiam, ut, cum ipse mihi imperet per apostolum suum et dicat ab episcopo refelli oportere teachers, quae non oportet (Tit 1,11), ego illorum indignationibus territus taceam. quod enim publicis gestis haerere uolui tam sacrilegum nefas, ad hoc utique uolui, ne me quisquam máxime in alus ciuitatíbus, ubi opportunum fuerit, ista deplorantem fingere aliquid arbitretur, quando etiam apud ipsam Hipponem iam dicitur non hoc Proculianum mandasse, quod publicum renuntiait officium. 5. Quid autem modestius agere possumus, quam ut tam grauem causam per te tamen agam, uirum et clarissima dignitate praeditum et consideratissima uoluntate tranquillum? peto igitur, sicut iam petiui per fratres us, bonds atque honest uiros, quos ad tuam eximie-

tatem misi, ut quaerere digneris, utrum Proculiani presbyter Victor non hoc [26] ab episcopo suo mandatum acceperit, quod officio publico renuntiauit, an forte, cum et ipse Victor aliud dixerit, falsum illi apud acta prosecuti sint, cum sint communionis eiusdem; aut, si consentit, ut ipsam totam quaestionem dissensionis nostrae placide pertractemus, ut error, qui iam manifestus est, manifestius innotescat, libenter amplector. audiui enim, quod dixerit, ut sine tumultu populan adsint nobiscum deni ex utraque parte graues et honesti uiri et secundum scripturas, quid in uero sit, perquiramus. nam illud, quod rursus eum dixisse nonnulli ad me pertulerunt, cur non ierim Constantinam, quando ibi plures ipsi erant, uel me deben iré Mileum, quod illic, sicut perhibent, concilium proxime habituri sunt, ridiculum est dicere, quasi ad me pertineat cuta propria nisi Hipponíensis ecclesiae. mihi tota huius quaestionis ratio máxime cum Proculiano est. sed si forte inparem se putat, cuius uoluerit, collegae sui inploret auxilium. in aliis enim ciuitatíbus tantum agimus, quod ad ecclesiam pertinet, quantum uel nos permittunt uel nobis inponunt earundem ciuitatum episcopi, fratres et consacerdotes nostri. 6. Quamquam et iste, qui se tot annorum episcopum dicit, quid me tirane timeat, quominus mecum uelit conferre sermonem non satis intellego: si doctrinam liberalium litterarum, quas forte ipse aut non

the doctrine of the liberal disciplines, if he did not learn them or learned them poorly? This question must be aired by the authority of the Holy Scriptures or by the ecclesiastical and public documents, which he has handled for so many years; In this he must be more skilled than me. Anyway, here is my brother and colleague Sansucio, bishop of the church of Turres, who has not studied those disciplines that Proculeiano fears, as he says. Come and discuss with him. I will plead with my colleague, and I trust in the name of Christ that he will easily agree. Sansucio will replace me, and the Lord him, in the fight for the truth, as I hope. He is not select in speech, although he is instructed in the true faith. Therefore, there is no excuse for transferring the dispute to I don't know who, to prevent us from dealing with it among ourselves, to whom it is up to us to do it. But, as I tell you, I don't shy away from the others either, if Proculeiano asks for their help. didicit aut minus didicit, quid hoc pertinet ad eam quaestíonem, quae uel de sanctís scripturis uel documentis ecclesiasticis aut publicis discutienda est, in quibus ille per tot annos uersatur, unde in eis debenet [27] esse pe(134)ritioi? desserto est hic frater et collega meus Samsucius, episcopus Turrensis ecclesiae, qui nullas such didicit, quales iste dicitur formidare; ipse adsit, agat ciim illo; rogabo eum et, ut confido in nomine Christi, facile mihi concedet, ut suscipiat in hac re uícem meam, et eum dominus pro ueritate certantem, quamuis sermone inpolitum, tamen uera fide eruditum, sicut confidimus, adiuuabit. nulla ergo causa est, cur ad alios nescio quos differat a, ne inter nos, quod ad nos pertinet, peragamus. nec tamen, ut dixi, etiam illos defugio, si eorum ipse poscit auxilium. a] deferat PL

Date: Year 396. Place: Hippo. Topic: Donatist controversy. AUGUSTINE aEUSEBIO, distinguished lord and worthy of welcome and most beloved brother. 1. I was not the annoying one who, with suggestions and requests, forced you against your will to judge, as you say, between two bishops. If I had wanted to convince you, I could have shown, perhaps easily, how you are qualified to judge between us in such a clear and manifest cause and what it is that you do; You who are so afraid to judge, do not hesitate to pass judgment in favor of one of the parties without having heard the other. But this, as I said, I will ignore for the moment. I had not asked for your honorable kindness - I hope you finally understand it with this letter! - but that you should ask Proculeianus if he had actually said to his priest Victor what public fame announced as having been said by him. Perhaps the emissaries did not record what they heard from Victor, but instead recorded a falsehood in the minutes. Finally, I wanted to know what Proculeiano thought about a possible discussion of this entire conflict between us. It seems to me that someone who is asked to ask someone and deign to send the answer is not constituted as a judge. XXXV [CSEL 34/2.27]
DOMINO EXIMIO MERITOQUE SUSCIPIENDO ET DILECTISSIMO FRATRI EUSEBIO AUGUSTINUS

1. Non ego recusanti uoluntati tuae iudicium, sicut dicis, inter episcopos subeundum molestus exhortator aut deprecator inposui. quod quidem etiam si suadere uoluissem, possem fortasse facile ostendere, quam ualeas iudicare inter nos in tam manifesta atque aperta causa et quale sit illud, quod facis, ut non auditis partibus iam ferré non dubites pro una parte sententiam, qui iudicium reformidas. sed hoc, ut dixi, interim omitto. nihil autem rogaueram aliud honorabilem benignitatem tuam, quod quaeso tandem in hac saltem epistula digneris aduertere, nisi ut quaereres a Proculiano, utrum hoc ipse dixerit Victori presbytero suo, quod ab eo sibi [28] dictum publicum officium renuntiauit, an forte, qui missi sunt, non quod a Victore audierunt, sed falsum gestis prosecuti sint; deinde quid illi de tota ipsa quaestione inter nos discuss uideretur. arbitror autem non iudicem fieri eum, qui rogatur, ut interroget aliquem et, quod ei responsum fuerit, rescribere dignetur. hoc

I return, then, to beg you to take the courage to do so, since Proculeianus refuses to receive my letters, as I know from experience. If he received them, I would surely not use your eminence. But, if he does not agree, can I try a gentler procedure than consulting him through a person like you, since you love him, and my position prohibits me from inhibiting myself? You say that the event of the mother being beaten by her son was displeasing to your seriousness. But you add that, if Proculeiano knew, he would separate such a sacrilegious young man from his communion. To that I answer briefly: now you know; separate it. 2. I will also add another thing: a former deacon of the Hispanic church, called Primo, was prohibited from approaching the nuns' convent. For having disregarded the healthy and orderly precepts, he was removed from the clergy. Angry against God's discipline, he went over to the Donatists and was rebaptized. Two other nuns, who belonged, like him, to the Catholic Christian camp, were dragged away, or they went after him. They were also renamed. Now they are with the circumcelions parties, with those wandering packs of women who do not want to have husbands because they do not submit to discipline. Now they proudly enjoy themselves in Bacchic rejoicings and abominable drunkenness, celebrating that they have been authorized to carry out this licentious and perverse conduct, which the Catholic Church prohibited. And perhaps Proculeiano ignores it. ergo etiam nunc rogo, ut faceré non graueris, quia litteras meas, sicut etiam expertus sum, non uult accipere. quod si uoluisset, non utique per tuam eximietatem id agerem. cum autem id non uult, quid possum mitius agere, quam ut per te, talem uirum et qui eum diligis, interrogetur aliquid, unde me tacere mea sarcina prohibet? quod autem mater a filio caesa tuae grauitati displicuit, sed "ille" dixisti "si sciret, a communione sua tam nefarium iuuenem prohibiturus esset", breuiter respondero: moda cognouit, moda prohibeat. 2.

Addo etiam aliud. subdiaconus quondam Spaniensis ecclesiae uocabulo Primus cum ab accessu indisciplinato sanctimoníalium prohiberetur atque ordinata et sana praecepta contemneret, a clericatu remotus est et ipse inritatus aduersus disciplinan] dei transtulit se ad illos et rebaptizatus est. duas etiam (135) sanctimoniales concolonas suas de fundo catholicorum Christianorum siue idem transtulit siue illum secutae etiam ipsae tamen rebaptizatae sunt et nunc cum gregibus Circumcellionum inter uagabundos greges feminarum, quae proterue* maritos habere noluerunt, ne habeant disciplinam, [29] in detestabilis uinolentiae bacchationibus superbus exultat gaudens latissimam sibi apertam esse licentiam malae conuersationis, unde in catholica prohibebatur. et hoc fortasse Proculianus ignorat. ergo per tuam grauitatem atque modestiam a] propterea PL

I wish to bring this to your attention through your gravity and modesty. May he order that anyone who has chosen it exclusively because he has lost the clerical status among Catholics due to his disobedience and corrupt customs be separated from your communion. 3. As long as it pleases God, I keep this rule: if someone wants to become Catholic and is degraded by ecclesiastical discipline, I receive him and humiliate him with the penance that the Donatists themselves would impose on him if he wanted to remain in their sect. See, then, please, how execrable their behavior is, when these whom, within the ecclesiastical discipline, we correct for their bad life, they induce them to receive another baptism; To deserve to receive it they require them to answer that they are pagans. How much blood of martyrs was shed so that that word did not come from Christian lips! Afterwards, the rebaptized consider themselves renewed and sanctified and, worsening in the discipline they could not tolerate, they rejoice in the sacrilege of their new fury under the appearance of a new grace. If I do wrong, let your benevolence correct this error. No one will complain about me if I let Proculeian know it by means of a public document, which I cannot be denied in a Roman city, I believe. God commands that we speak and preach the word, that we refute those who teach what is not appropriate, that we insist with or without opportunity; I can prove it with the words of the Lord or the apostles. Nobody thinks that they are going to silence me about these eidem in notitiam perferatur. iubeat eum, qui non ob aliud illam communionem delegit, nisi quia in catholica clericatum amiserat propter inoboedientiam et perditos mores, a sua communione remoueri. 3.

Etenim ego, si domino placet, istum modum seruo, ut, quisquís apud eos propter disciplinam degradatus ad catholicam transiré uoluerit, in humiliatione paenitentiae recipiatur, quo et ipsi eum forsitan cogerent, si apud eos manere uoluisset. ab eis uero consider, quaeso te, quam execrabiliter fiat, ut, quos male uiuentes ecclesiastica disciplina corripimus, persuadeatur eis, ut ad lauacrum alterum ueniant atque, ut id accipere mereantur, pagans se esse responder, quae uox ne proceedet de ore Christiano, tantus sanguis martyrum fusus est, deinde quasi renouati et quasi sanctificati disciplinae, quam ferré non potuerunt, deteriores facti sub specie nouae gratiae sacrilege noui furoris insultent. aut si male fació per tuam beniuolentiam ista corrigenda curare, de me nullus queratur, si haec illi perferri in notitiam per codices publices fecero, qui mihi negari, ut arbitror, ​​in Romana ciuitate non possunt. nam cum deus imperet, ut loquamur et praedicemus uerbum et teachers, quae non oporteat, refellamus et instemus opportune atque importune (cf. 2 Tim 4,2; Tit 1,11), [30] sicuti dominicis et apostolicis litteris probo, nullus hominum mihi silentium de his rebus persuadendum arbitre-

points. If the Donatists consider themselves bold enough to proceed as revolutionaries and robbers, the Lord will not fail to protect his Church. In its womb, expanded throughout the world, it has already subjected all kingdoms to its yoke. 4. There is a certain settler of the Church here who had a catechumen daughter in our communion. She was seduced into coming to them, against the will of her parents, to be baptized, and she adopted the profession of a nun. Her father wanted to make her return with severity to the Catholic communion. But I refused to receive a woman with a corrupt mind, if she did not return spontaneously, choosing the best by her free will. The settler insisted that the daughter give her consent, even hitting her. At that moment I strictly forbade it. However, as I passed through Spaniano, a Donatist priest from that city met me, in the middle of the field of an honorable Catholic woman, shouting with an impudent voice after us that I was a traitor and persecutor. He also launched such insults against that honorable woman in whose field we were, and who belongs to our communion. When I heard those screams, I not only stopped myself from fighting, but I stopped the crowd that was accompanying me. However, if I propose: "Let's find out who the traitors and persecutors are," the answer is: "We don't want to dispute, we want to rebaptize; We dedicate ourselves to tearing your sheep to pieces like a wolf, with insidious teeth; You remain silent, if you are a good man. uiolenter autem uel latrocinanter si quid audendum putauerint, non deerit dominus ad tuendam ecclesiam suam, qui iugo suo in gremio eius toto orbe diffuso omnia terrena regna subiecit. 4.

Nam cum ecclesiae quidam colonus filiam suam, quae apud nos fuet catechumena et ad illos a seducta est inuitis parentibus, ut ibi baptizata etiam sanctimonalis formam susciperet, ad communionem catholícam paterna uellet seueritate reuocare et ego feminam corruptae mentís nisi uolentem et libero arbitrio meliora deligentem suscipi noluissem, ílle rusticus etiam plagis instare coepit, ut sibi filia consentiret. quod statim omni moda fieri prohibui. tamen per Spanianum transeuntibus nobis presbyter ipsíus stans in medio fundo catholicae ac laudabilis (136) feminae uoce inpudentissima post nos clamauit, quod traditores et persecutors essemus, quod conuicium etiam in illam feminam iaculatus est, quae communionis est nostrae, in cuius medio fundo stabat. quibus uocibus auditis non solum me ipsum a lite refrenaui. sed etiam multitudinem, quae mihi comitabatur, compescui. et tamen si dicam: quaeratur, qui sint uel fuerint traditores uel persecutors, respondtur mihi: will dispute nolumus et rebaptizare uolumus; nos oues oues insidiantibus morsibus luporum more depraedemur, uos, si boni pastores estis, a] ab illis Í>L

shepherd. What else has Proculeyan ordered, if anything? «If you are a Christian, he says, leave this dispute to the judgment of God, if we do not resolve it; "You shut up." The same priest took the liberty of threatening the administrator who cultivates the Church's property. 5. I beg you to let all this come to Proculeian's knowledge through you: let him moderate the frenzy of his clerics, which forces me to address you, honorable Eusebius. Deign to let me know, not what you feel about all of this, so that you do not imagine that I impose the responsibility of judge on you, but what they think. May the mercy of God keep you safe, exemplary lord, and I justly accept.

Date: After April 397. Place: Hippo. Topic: Rebuttal of a writing about fasting on the Sabbath. AUGUSTINE wishes health in the Lord to CASULANO, a dearly loved, dearly loved and compassionate brother. 11. I don't know what it was like not to answer your first letter, but I know that I didn't stop doing it out of disdain for you, please contact yourself—quid enim aliud mandauit Proculianus, si uere ipse mandauit?—[31] if Christianus is, serua hoc iudicio dei, nisi nos faciamus; tu tace ausus etiam idem presbyter homini rusticano conductori fundi ecclesia^ comminari. 5. Haec quoque omnia per te, quaeso, nouerit Proculianus; cohetceat insaniam clericorum suorum, unde, honorabilis Eusebi, non apuw te tacui. digberis itaque, non quid tu de his omnibuss felt, ne tih¡ arbitreris a me juudicis onus inponi, sed quid illi responder, mih, ¡ rescribere. Misericordia dei te incolumem tueatur, domine eximie ^. merit sustains ac dilectissime frater. XXXVI [CSEL 34/2,31]
DiLECTISSIMO ET DESIDERANTISSIMO FRATRI ET CONPRESBYTERO CASULANK AUGUSTINUS IN DOMINO SALUTEM ^
I 1. Nescio, unde sit factum, ut primis tuis litteris meas non rert derem; non tamen tui contemptu id fecisse me scio; nam et studiis tuj s

Your studies and your word delight me so much and I so desire that in the flower of your age you progress in the knowledge of the word of God and abound for the edification of the Church: I urge you to do so. Upon now receiving this letter, by which with fraternal and just right of charity, in which we are one, you demand that I finally answer you, I thought that I could no longer defer to your pleasure the fulfillment of that wish, and among my very narrow occupations I take this to answer you properly to justify myself with you. 2. You ask me if it is lawful to fast on the Sabbath. I answer that, if it were not lawful, neither Moses, nor Elijah, nor the Lord himself would have fasted for forty days in a row. It is clear that for this reason it is concluded that it is also licit to fast on Sunday, and, however, if one judges that one should fast on Sunday as some keep the Sabbath fast, it will rightly cause no small scandal in the Church. In these matters, in which nothing certain is recorded in the divine Scripture, the custom of the people of God or the observance of the elders must be maintained as law. If I began to dispute about such matters and argue with some with the custom of others, I would cause endless litigation; but I will not find any true document, no matter how much I talk; This must be avoided so as not to darken the peace of charity with a stormy strife. 23. I do not have so much time that I can use it to refute each of your sentences, since I need it to draft other more urgent treaties. But you have shown me in your letters great ingenuity, and I love in you that gift of God. Consider, then, more diligently that treatise of the Urbicus i ^ and you will see that it does not spare the insults to almost the entire Church of Christ, from east to west. Better said, he does not wound the whole case, but the whole of it, since he has not forgiven the Romans themselves, whose custom he believes he defends. In the impetuosity of his insults, he inadvertently ignores that they also redound against the Romans themselves. When he lacks arguments to prove that one must fast on Saturday, he insolently launches into condemning clumsy drunkenness, sybaritis, food and licentious feasts, as if the purpose of fasting were as much as getting drunk. And if that is so, what good is it for the Romans to fast on Saturday? On other days you do not fast; Therefore, according to his arguments, in those days we must consider them drunks and sybarites. It is one thing to burden the heart with profligacy and drunkenness, which is always bad, and another to mitigate the fast, eating with modesty and temperance; This is what no Christian disapproves of when doing Sunday. Therefore, first distinguish the meals of the saints from the voracity and drunkenness of the slaves of the womb; thus he will not include among these the Romans unless II 3.

We do wrong when we eat, we do not live well on any Sunday. And since he confesses that the apostles ate on the Sabbath, he argues that then it was not the time to fast, because the Lord said: The days will come when the husband will be taken away from them, and then the husband's children will fast, and that there is a time for joy and a time for mourning. But he should have noticed first that the Lord speaks in that passage about fasting in general and not about Sabbath fasting. He wants to identify mourning with fasting and joy with food. Whatever God meant by saying that he rested on the seventh day from all his works, it does not mean mourning, but joy. Why don't you notice it? Unless you say that this rest of God and sanctification of the Sabbath means joy for Jews and mourning for Christians. When the Lord sanctified the seventh day, because on it he rested from all his works, he said nothing about fasting or eating. When he spoke to the Hebrew people about keeping the Sabbath, he also did not mention the foods they were to eat or not eat. It only prescribed abstention from menial work. The Hebrew people accepted this precept, which was a symbol of future rest, and abstained from working: we see that the Jews still abstain from working on the Sabbath, although the carnal Jews do not understand what the Christians correctly understand. It says that the Apostles ate on the Sabbath, because the time had not yet come to fast on that day: that fast was prohibited in the tradition of the ancients. Be careful, then, lest we answer in a timely manner, saying that for some reason the Lord wanted his disciples to do both things on that day: pluck the ears of grain and eat the food; the first, against those who want to rest on Saturday, and the second, against those who force fasting on Saturday; Thus the Lord made it clear that the first was superstition, once the times changed, and the second was free at all times. I would say this with greater reason than the propositions he establishes. 47. He continues: "How can we not be condemned with the Pharisee, since we fast twice a week?" As if the Pharisee had been condemned because he fasted twice a week and not because he proudly put himself before the publican! With the same reason I could affirm that those who give a tenth of their income to the poor must be condemned with the Pharisee, since he boasted of this among other works. We would like many Christians to do so, since we only find a few who imitate that Pharisee. Likewise, we would say that anyone who is not an adulterer, unjust or a thief will be condemned with the Pharisee because he boasted that he was not. Surely whoever says that is crazy. These undoubted goods that the Pharisee boasted of possessing should not be aired with that proud boasting with which he did so; but they must be treated with that humble piety that was missed in him. In the same way, it is useless for someone like that Pharisee to fast twice a week, but it is religious for a humbly faithful or faithfully humble man to do so. Apart from that the Evangelical Scripture did not say that the Pharisee was condemned, but rather that the publican was justified. 8. Pharisees and publicans, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven. As if we couldn't fulfill that precept if we fasted only twice a week! There are seven days that in their temporal revolution constitute time; If we remove two, Saturday and Sunday, for fasting, there are five days left, in which a subject can surpass the Pharisee who fasts twice a week. In my opinion, if one fasts three times a week, he already surpasses the Pharisee, who only fasts twice. And if one fasts four times a week or five, except on Saturday and Sunday (many do so throughout their lives, especially in monasteries), then he is not only superior in the fatigue of fasting to the Pharisee, who fasted twice a week, but also to the Christian, who is accustomed to fasting on Wednesday, Friday and Saturday, as the Roman people frequently do. On the other hand, that discussant calls someone carnal who fasts for five consecutive days and does not repair the body at all. As if only on other days food and drink had nothing to do with meat! What's more, he believes that he who fasts those five days in a row is a servant of his belly, as if only the food on Saturday went to the belly. 59. It is not enough for him to surpass the Pharisee by fasting three times a week, but he forces him to fast six days, excepting only Sunday, for he says: "Once

the old defilement and remaining in one flesh under the discipline of Christ, they must no longer dedicate themselves (without law, together with their children, with the princes of Sodom and with the populace of Gomorrah) to the sensual feasts of the Sabbath; We must legitimately fast more and more, within the solemn and ecclesiastical law, with the cultivators of holiness and with those consecrated to God, thus purifying in the sources of fasting, almsgiving and prayer any error, however slight, of the six days; and thus strengthened by the Sunday prayer, we can all sing with a uniform heart and with dignity: You satisfied, Lord, the hungry soul and you watered the thirsty soul. By speaking in this way, and excepting only Sunday from fasting, he blindly and carelessly accuses not only the Christian peoples of the East and West, but also the Roman Church itself. He affirms that "remaining under the discipline of Christ, they should no longer dedicate themselves (without law, together with their children, with the princes of Sodom and with the populace of Gomorrah) to the sensual feasts of the Sabbath, but they must legitimately fast more and more, within the solemn and ecclesiastical right, with the cultivators of holiness and with those consecrated to God." He then explains what it means to fast legitimately, adding: "purifying in the sources of fasting, almsgiving and prayer any error, however slight, of the six days." That is to say, he believes that those who fast less than six days a week are not legitimately practicing fasting, nor are they consecrated to God, nor purified.

Who will be found who practices daily fasting in all these six days except a few clerics and monks? Especially considering that, apparently, in Rome they do not fast on Thursday. 10. Then I ask: if an error, even slight, on any day, is forgiven and cleansed by the fast of that day, since it says that "any error, even slight, of the six days is purified in the fountains of fasting," what will we do about that error that creeps in on Sunday, on which day fasting cannot be done without scandal? Or, if on that day no Christian errs, let that man, who pretends to be a great faster, to brand others as slaves of the belly, see the honor and usefulness that he attributes to that belly, since, according to him, when you eat you do not err. Is it that he places such an effective good in the Sabbath fast that only the Sabbath fast can erase the slight error of the other six days, including Sunday? Is error only avoided on Saturday, because on it one fasts entirely? Why does he put Sunday before Saturday, as if relying on Christian law? Behold, according to him, Saturday is much holier than Sunday, since on the former there is no error if the total fast is kept; Furthermore, by fasting on Saturday the error of the other six days is erased, including Sunday therefore. I think you don't like that position.

11. He wants to pass himself off as a spiritual man, and denounces those who eat on the Sabbath as carnal. But look how Sunday is not content with a meager meal, but delights in praise. What is alogia, a word taken from the Greek language, but to give oneself over to food, deviating from the norms of reason? Animals, which lack reason, are called analogues, and those who devote themselves to the stomach are similar to them. That is why the immoderate feast is called alogia, because greed in food and drink clouds the mind, in which reason reigns. Furthermore, he affirms that because of food and drink, that is, not of the mind, but of the belly, it is necessary to sing in the Sunday alogia: You satisfied, Lord, the hungry soul and you watered the thirsty soul. Oh spiritual man! Oh prosecutor of the carnal! Oh great faster and no ventriculturist! Behold, he warns us not to corrupt the law of the Lord with the law of the womb and not to sell the bread of heaven for earthly food, adding "because by food Adam perished in paradise and by food Esau lost his birthright." See who says: «The temptation of the belly is the well-known trick of Satan: he advises a little to remove everything. The observance of these precepts does not succeed in bending the ventricians. 12. Doesn't it seem that with those words he intends to fast on Sunday as well? Otherwise, the Sabbath, on which the Lord rested in the tomb, will be holier than Sunday.

nec maculas erroris, quae de ista mor [39] talitate contrahuntur, abluere. uideant ergo Romani, quid agant, quia etiam ipsi nimium contumeliose huius disputatione tractantur, apud quos ómnibus istis sex diebus praeter paucissimos clericos aut monachos quotusquisque inuenitur, qui frequentet everyday ieiunia, máxime quia ibi ieiunandum quinta sabbati non uidetur? 10. testimony of the Acts of the Apostles, when the apostle Paul was in Troas. There it reads: On the first day of the week we gathered together for the breaking of bread, and Paul argued with them, ready to leave the next day; and the conversation lasted until midnight. Paul came down from the upper room, where everyone was gathered, to resurrect the adolescent who, heavy with sleep, had fallen from a window and was carried away dead; Then the Scripture continues speaking of the Apostle: When Paul went up, after having broken the bread and having tasted it, he continued speaking until dawn, and so he broke. God forbid we should understand the text as if the Apostles had been in the habit of fasting solemnly on the Lord's Day. It is true that what we call Sunday today was called the first day of the week, which is seen more clearly in the Gospels. In fact, the day of the Lord's resurrection is called by Saint Matthew the first day of the week, and by the other evangelists, one of the week; and it is clear that that day is what we call Sunday. Perhaps they had gathered at the beginning of the night, after the Sabbath had passed, in which case that night already belongs to Sunday, that is, to the first day of the week. In this hypothesis the bread was broken that night, as it is broken in the sacrament of the body of Christ; The conversation continued until midnight and then Paul continued speaking to those gathered there until dawn. Paul had

hurry, having to leave at dawn on Sunday. Or perhaps, if they had met during the day and not during the night of Sunday, the reason for the prolonged conversation is expressed, namely, that he had to leave and wanted to leave them sufficiently instructed, when it is explained: Paul argued with them, ready to leave the next day. In this case they did not fast solemnly on Sunday, but rather they did not see fit to interrupt with dinner a necessary conversation, to which everyone listened with ardor and enthusiastic eagerness; The Apostle had to leave, who could never or rarely visit them, to attend other trips around the world. We must especially take into account that Paul had to leave that region to no longer see them in the flesh, as the following context proves. Therefore it seems that they were not in the habit of fasting on Sundays, and, in order to be believed, the author of the book took care to express the reason for the prolonged conversation. Thus it teaches us that, when a need arises, food should not be put before a more urgent activity. This eager audience, thinking that the fountain itself was going to move away, so attentive to drinking what flowed from it, to quench its great thirst, not for water, but for the word, not only disdained carnal food, but also dinner. 29. Although at that time they did not have the custom of fasting on Sunday, it did not cause much offense to the Church by neglecting the restoration of the body in such a need as that which confronted the apostle Paul, throughout the Sunday.

Why does the Church fast mainly on Wednesdays and Fridays? The reason seems to be that, according to the Gospel, on the fourth day of the week, which we commonly call the fourth day, the Jews gathered together to kill the Lord. And since no angry person finds his anger unfair, it slips away. Then the inveterate anger turns into hatred, and, while a certain satisfaction is mixed with the just pain, the interested party retains it for a long time in the glass, until the contents turn sour and the glass becomes contaminated. Therefore, not being angry at anyone, not even with reason, is much better than slipping into hatred due to that mysterious lubricity of anger when we become angry with apparent justice. We often say, when receiving unknown guests, that it is better to tolerate a bad individual than, for fear of receiving the bad one, perhaps to exclude the good one without knowing it. But in the feelings of the soul the opposite happens. For it is incomparably better not to open the tabernacle of the heart to the righteous anger that calls, than to admit it, for it will not go away easily, but will turn from a branch to a beam. Those who do not defend their sentence with stubborn animosity, even if it is perverse and false, are considered heretics; especially if they did not invent it out of their own audacious presumption, but were seduced and led into error, because they received it from their parents, and provided that they also seek the truth with prudent diligence and are willing to correct themselves when they find it. If I didn't believe that you were one of those, perhaps I wouldn't send you a letter. It is true that we are exhorted to shun the heretic swollen by his hateful pride and maddened by his fatal and contentious stubbornness, so that he does not seduce the weak and small; but I also do not refuse to correct him with all the means that I discover at my disposal. That is why I have also written to some of the Donatist leaders, not letters of communion, since for a long time they have not received them from the universal Catholic unity due to their perversity, but private letters, such as I could lawfully send them to the pagans. They have read them; However, either they did not want to or, as seems more credible, they could not answer. By sending them, it seemed to me that I fulfilled my duty of charity, as imposed on us, not only towards our own, but towards everyone, by the Holy Spirit when he told us through the Apostle: May the Lord multiply and increase your charity, not only among yourselves, but towards everyone. He also admonishes us in another passage to gently correct those who disagree with our doctrine, saying: Perhaps the Lord will give them repentance to

know the truth, and discover the snares of the devil, of whom you are captive under his will. 2. Let me, therefore, serve as a defense testimony before the court of God, who knows my intention, and who said: Blessed are the peaceful, for they will be called children of God. 23. The cause of Felix Aptungitanus was also aired at that council, with much greater hostility and malice than the others. After reading everything, I replied: it was no wonder that the promoters of the schism rashly judged that they should condemn them. The emulators and losers pressed against the victims, drawing up the corresponding report. I stated that, by the way, the prisoners were absent and did not know about the lawsuit. It is not about your gold or silver, nor the land, nor the estates, nor is it even discussed about the health of your body. I call your souls so that you may achieve eternal life and avoid eternal death. Wake up at once. I am not introducing you to a dark question. I do not reveal to you dark secrets, for whose penetration human reason is not enough, at least ordinary reason. The matter is clear. What is more noticeable? What do you see the soonest? I say that the innocent and absent were condemned by a reckless council, even if it was very numerous, and I prove it with the proconsular acts: in these the one whom the acts of a council, adduced by yours, declared a high degree of criminal, was judged free of all crime. I say that the sentences were pronounced by confessed traditors against some alleged traditors; and I prove it with the ecclesiastical records in which the names are given; According to these, Segundo Tigisitano dismissed, in attention to peace, those causes that he knew; but then he broke the peace and condemned those whose causes he did not know. From which it is discovered that in the first part Segundo did not act out of love for peace, but out of personal fear. Because Purpúreo Limatense had reproached him for the fact that he was also detained, by official order and the bailiff, to hand over the Scriptures, and he was

then released; Without a doubt, he was not let off the hook, but because he delivered or had something delivered. Segundo Tigisitano having this suspicion quite well founded, accepted the advice of Segundo the Lesser, his blood relative; He consulted the other bishops who were with him, left obvious crimes to God's judgment, and thus gave the impression that he sought peace. But that was false, since he was looking out for his own safety. 7. If he had had the thought of peace in his heart, he would not have joined later with the traitors, whom he had referred to God when he had them present and confessed, to condemn as guilty of the surrender of the sacred books those who were absent, and whom no one had declared guilty in his presence. With all the more reason he must have feared that the unity of peace would be broken, since the city of Carthage was large and famous. From there, the evil that originated there was to spill over, as from a vertex, throughout the African body. It was, furthermore, a famous and noble city, very close to the overseas regions. Their bishop had great authority and could not inhibit himself in the face of a conspiracy by the enemy crowd. They saw that Caecilian was united by letters of communion to the Roman church, in which the primacy of the apostolic chair always resided, and to the other regions through which the Gospel came to Africa itself; Caecilian was there ready to present his case if his enemies tried to separate him from his other colleagues. cough in the fog of false rumor. You see, dear ones, that what some of you said was implausible is possible. Those who confessed their betrayal and argued that it was better to leave their cause to God, are the same ones who later became judges and condemners of the alleged absent traitors. They took advantage of the opportunity to launch the false accusation against others; directing the conversation of men upon them, they so ingeniously avoided the investigation of their own crimes. If it were not possible for a true criminal to accuse another alleged offender of his own wickedness, would the apostle Paul not have said to some: Therefore you are inexcusable, O man, whoever you judge. Because in what you judge, you condemn yourself, since you do the same thing that you judge. That is precisely what they did, and that is why these apostolic words suit them completely and appropriately. 11. Then, when Segundo referred the crimes to God, he did not do it for peace and unity; With all the more reason he would have done it later in Carthage, where he was not forced to forgive any confessed convict present, so as not to give rise to a schism. To preserve peace, it was enough to refuse to condemn those who were absent, and that was very easy. Therefore, they would have done an injury to the innocent, even if they had wanted to forgive them, without being convicted or confessed and not even present. Only he whose guilt is manifest can receive forgiveness. How much more blind and cruel were they in believing that they could condemn what they could not even forgive without proof? In the first case, the unknown had been left to God, so as not to continue investigating; In the second, the unknown was condemned to cover up what was discovered. But someone will say: "They knew him." Even if I granted that, they should have forgiven those absent, who had not withdrawn from the trial, since they never attended it. The Church was not in those African bishops alone, to be able to say that whoever refused to appear at such a trial was exempt from any ecclesiastical trial. There were still thousands of transmarine colleagues who could judge those who were suspected before their African or Numidian colleagues. Scripture cries out: Before interrogation, revile no one; and when you have questioned, correct fairly. For if the Holy Spirit does not want to be reproached or corrected until after having been interrogated, how much more criminal will those be who were not content with reproaching and correcting, but who set out to condemn without having been able to interrogate those who were absent about their crimes? 12. Those absent had not abandoned the trial, because they never attended it; They always declared that such an assembly was suspicious to them. The Donatists say, however, that they condemned known crimes. My brothers, please, how did you know them? You will answer: "We do not know, since such knowledge is not explained in the minutes." But I will show you how they met them. Examine the case of Félix Aptungitano and notice first of all the vehemence

that they used against him. They knew, therefore, the cause of the others as well as that of this one, whose total innocence was demonstrated after a terrible and thorough investigation. With how much greater justice, certainty and promptness should we declare innocent those whose crimes the Donatists denounced with greater mildness and condemned with a more benign rebuke, when the one against whom they so cruelly cruelly was found blameless! 4 13. Someone said something that you found not very funny when you heard it, but that cannot be ignored. So this guy said: "A bishop should not have been declared innocent by a proconsular trial." As if that bishop had sought the sentence and they were not orders from the emperor, to whose tutelage this care belonged in the first place, for which he must give an account to God! It was the Donatists who made the emperor arbitrator and judge in the cause of the betrayal of the schism, when they sent him prayers and when they later appealed to him and, nevertheless, refused to submit to his ruling. Therefore, if the one who was acquitted by an earthly judge without having asked for it is guilty, how much more guilty will those who decided that an earthly judge be judge in the case? Those very serious men of the court preferred to listen to a tangle of infinite questions related to each other like an inextricable chain, without caring about the number of the bishops or where they came from. However, there you have the last sentence pronounced by the blessed Melquíades. How innocent and upright, how generous and peaceful! promoter of all evil. He left the others a free option to recover their health, willing to send letters of communion to those who had been consecrated by Mayorino, as was recorded. In all those places where there were two bishops constituted by the schism, he wanted to confirm the one who had been ordained previously, providing that the other was given the government of another flock. Oh optimal man! Oh son of Christian peace and father of the Christian people! Now compare this minority with that multitude of bishops; But do not compare the number, but the weight. On the one hand, modesty; on the other, recklessness; on the one hand, surveillance; on the other, stubbornness. There neither meekness corrupted integrity, nor integrity destroyed meekness; On the other hand, here fear was covered with fury, and fury was awakened by fear. Some had gathered to reject false crimes by examining the true ones, the others to conceal the true crimes by condemning the false ones. 6 17. Aaron tolerates the crowd that demands an idol, makes it and worships it. Moses tolerates so many thousands of murmurers against God, whose holy name they so often offend. David tolerates Saul, his persecutor, who renounces the heavenly for his clumsy customs and seeks the infernal with magical arts; avenges him when he was murdered, calling him at the same time Christ of the Lord through the sacrament of venerable anointing. Absent states are distinguished with the most vehement accusation. The judgment of the bishops is appealed to the emperor. The very judgment of the emperor is despised. Our best book is the earthly world: seeing come true what was prophesied in the book of God. This did not mean that we should distance ourselves from the Catholic communion if something happened against our will, and even despite our opposition, if we could resist. In Arzuges, as I have heard, the barbarians usually take an oath by their gods before the decurion of the border or before the tribune. They are hired to drive the cart or to take care of the products, so owners and settlers often hire them as loyalists, and travelers take them as trusted guides when they have a letter from the decurion. Now this doubt arises in my heart: the owner who hires a barbarian, whose loyalty seems firm, because he has sworn by his gods, is not himself stained, as well as his products, or the traveler for whom the barbarian serves as a guide? Keep in mind that the barbarian who pronounces the oath does so in favor of the owner, for taking care of the products, or in favor of the pedestrian, for his guide services; Despite the payment given by the owner and the traveler, a mortal oath is still required, sworn before the decurion or tribune. That is what makes me fear that whoever accepts the barbarian's oath will be contaminated, or that the fruits that the barbarian cares for will be contaminated. Precautions are taken, paying in gold, taking hostages, and yet that wicked oath is always asked. Please deign to give me a definitive and non-hesitant answer. Doubts as to whether we should benefit from the faith or fidelity of one who swears by the gods, who must maintain it. I ask you to consider, first of all, this: Do you not think that he who swears by false gods that he will keep the faith and then does not keep it sins twice? If he keeps the faith promised with that oath, we must judge that he sins only for having sworn by such gods. No one will rightly accuse him of not having kept his word. He who swore by those he should not have and also did what he should not have done against the promised faith, sinned twice. Donato's party, formed with only Africans, slanders the universe; He does not consider that, by refusing to produce fruits of peace and charity, he has separated himself, in his sterility, from that root of the Eastern churches from which the Gospel came to Africa. They worship the land if it is brought from the East, but they reject and rebaptize a believer if he comes from it. This also was predicted by the Son of God, the Truth: that He was the vine, that His children were the branches, and His Father the farmer. The branch that does not bear fruit in me, my Father will cut off; But the branch that bears fruit in me will be pruned so that it will bear more fruit. NOTE ON THE FOLLOWING TWO LETTERS'

The two books whose title is "To the Consultations of Jenaro" contain many lucubrations about the sacraments that are celebrated by the universal Church and by individuals, or that are not celebrated with a uniform tradition everywhere. Although I could not touch on all the points, I modestly satisfied my correspondent. The first of the two books is a letter, since the epigraph says who it is addressed to. In the list of books, I placed it as the first part of the next one, much more prolix and rich in content. In the first, speaking of manna, I affirm "that it tasted to each man's palate according to his desire." I can't find anything to prove it with, except with the Book of Wisdom, which for the Jews has no canonical authority. In any case, the phenomenon had to be limited to faithful Jews; It could not affect those who murmured against the Lord, since they would not have desired other delicacies, if the taste of the manna had depended on their taste. The book begins this way: "I would like you to answer yourself..."
AUGUSTINE greets JENARUS, his most beloved son, in the Lord (Book I).

11. I would like you yourself to answer whoever asks you what you ask me. That way I could satisfy you more quickly, approving or amending your answers, and thus confirm or correct you easily. I would prefer it, as I say. But, to answer you for the moment, I had to lengthen this letter 7, rather than delay the time of answering. First of all, I want you to retain what is main in this debate, namely: that Our Lord Jesus Christ, as He Himself says in His Gospel, has subjected us to His easy yoke and His light burden. Apostle. The Savior, to recommend with greater interest the excellency of the Sacrament, wanted it to be the last thing to be recorded in the hearts and memories of the disciples, from whom he was going to separate to go to the passion. But he did not order that a fixed order be maintained from now on, reserving that function to the apostles, by whom he was going to organize the churches. If Christ had commanded that the Sacrament always be received after meals, I believe that no one would have changed such custom. The Apostle, when speaking of this Sacrament, said: Therefore, brothers, when you come together to eat, show mutual deference. If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, so that you do not gather to your condemnation. And then he adds: I will arrange the rest when it arrives. From which we must understand that he imposed what does not vary with diversity of customs; It was already too much to want to establish in a letter all that order of practice that the universal Church maintains. 79. But I believe that it is celebrated with greater piety so that those who fast can also approach the Sacrament afterward.

17. Now we walk in faith and in hope of what, as I explained above, we try to achieve with love: a holy and perpetual rest from all fatigue and all discomfort. We make the transition to that rest from this life, which our Lord Jesus Christ deigned to announce and consecrate in his passion. In that rest there does not reign a lazy laziness, but rather an ineffable tranquility of restful activity. At last one rests from the works of this life, to begin to enjoy the activity of the other. Such activity is employed in the praise of God, without fatigue of limbs, without craving for worries; one does not enter it through rest so that fatigue follows; That is, it does not begin to be activity in such a way that it ceases to be rest. No more working and worrying; It remains in activity which produces rest, without working in fatigue or hesitating in thoughts. And since through this rest one returns to the primitive life, from which the soul fell by sinning, that rest is symbolized in the Sabbath. If you look at the seven days of Genesis, you will find that the seventh has no evening, because it symbolizes endless rest. The ancient people were commanded to celebrate the Sabbath physically with leisure, so that it would be a figure of sanctification in the rest of the Holy Spirit. Thus, we never read in Genesis that sanctification is represented by the other previous days, but only about the Sabbath it is said: And the Lord sanctified the seventh day. Both pious and wicked souls love rest; but they totally ignore the path by which they reach the goal they love. Even bodies, with their corresponding gravity, tend towards the same thing that souls tend towards with their love. The body, with its own weight, tends up or down, until it reaches the place to which it tends, and then rests; If the oil is spilled into the air, it goes downwards under its own weight; but if it is spilled under water, it goes upwards; In the same way, souls tend toward those things they love, precisely to reach them and rest. There are many things that delight because of the body, but in them there is no eternal rest, not even lasting rest; That is why they rather dirty the soul and recharge it; They counteract the specific weight of the soul, which carries it upwards. When the soul delights in itself, it does not yet delight in an unalterable thing; That is why it is still arrogant, because it is considered the highest, being so

Through the Holy Spirit we are given that mentioned rest that we love everywhere and nowhere do we find except by loving God, when his charity is diffused in our hearts by the Holy Spirit, which has been given to us. Remember well what I said before, namely, that through hope we have been saved, and the hope that is seen is not hope. 21. All these things that are figuratively preached to us

They have the mission of nourishing and fostering that fire of love that, like a specific weight, pushes us inward and upward to take us to rest. They promote and ignite love much more than if they were offered naked, without any sacramental resemblance. It is difficult to find out the cause of this phenomenon. But it is a fact that, when something with an allegorical meaning is proposed to us, it moves us, delights us and is honored more than if it were stated plainly in its own words. I believe that this movement of the soul is kindled with greater difficulty while we are still entangled in earthly things. If the bodily similarities are presented to it and from them the reference is made to the spiritual ones, which are symbolized in such images, the fire feels strengthened in that same transit. It is like the fire of a brand, which ignites when shaken. Thus the soul is carried away to rest with the most ardent love. 12 22. This is why, among the ten precepts, only the one that refers to the Sabbath is ordered to be figuratively observed. This figure is proposed to us so that we understand it, but not so that we celebrate it with bodily rest. On the other hand, the other precepts must be observed properly, as they were commanded, without any other figurative meaning. We have simply learned not to worship idols, not to receive the name of the Lord our God in vain, to honor father and mother, not to commit adultery, not to kill, not to steal, not to bear false witness, not to desire our neighbor's wife and not to covet any of his goods. In all of them one thing is not presented figuratively and another is mystically meant, but rather they are observed as they sound. On the other hand, we are not commanded to observe the Sabbath to the letter with regard to the suspension of bodily activity, as the Jews observe; literal observance, which is considered ridiculous, unless it means another certain spiritual rest. We understand, therefore, with reason, that all those things that are told to us figuratively in the Holy Scriptures are valid to inflame the love for which we tend to rest, since in the Decalogue only the precept of rest is figuratively proposed, which is loved everywhere and only in God is it found with certainty and holiness. 13 23. Sunday was prescribed, not to the Jews, but to the Christians, because of the resurrection of the Lord, and from that moment on it began to have its solemnity. It does not suspend, but glorifies that rest. When the body is returned, it does not bring with it its miseries, because it does not bring corruption: It is appropriate that this corruptible be clothed with incorruption and this mortal be clothed with immortality. The holy patriarchs, full of prophetic spirit before the resurrection of the Lord, already knew that sacrament of the eighth day which means the resurrection. The reason is that at that time the rest of the dead was given, but there could not be talk of resurrection of anyone who, upon rising from the dead, no longer died and death did not dominate him. It seems that you must make such progress that you can confidently await the last day of this temporary smoke or vapor called human life, and which no mortal can avoid; I trust that you await it with eagerness and security, or at least without desperate concern, founded not on the vanity of error, but on the solidity of truth. Given your nature, I cannot doubt that you will easily escape this custom of the Donatists, if in your religion you do not despise Christian purity. Even the slow-witted can see, just by listening with patience and attention, the indisputable and documented support with which this error is refuted. Now to continue with unaccustomed righteousness and break the bond of usual and familiar perversity requires greater strength. But with the help and exhortation of God our Lord, there is no need to despair of your generous freedom and your truly virile chest. May the mercy of God our Lord preserve you unscathed, excellent lord, truly honorable and most beloved son. such te prouectus habiturum, ut huius fumi uel uaporis temporalis, quae uita humano dicitur (cf.

Iac 4,15), ultimum diem, quem nulli mortalium euitare conceditur, uel auidus uel securus uel certe non desperate sollicitus non in uanitate erroris sed in soliditate ueritatis expectes. quam certum est enim tibi uiuere te, tam sit certum doctrina salutari istam uitam, quae in deliciis temporalibus agitur, in comparatione uitae aeternae, quae nobis per Christum atque in Christo promittitur, non uitam sed mortem esse deputandam. nullo moda autem dubitauerim de indole tua, quod ista consuetudine Donatistarum facillime te extrahes, si religiosissime ipsam Christianam puritatem non paruipenderis. quam inconcussis (224) enim documentum firmamentis error ille conuincatur, non magnum est etiam tardis ingenio, si tantum patienter atque attempt audierint, peruidere. sed ad sectandam insolitam rectitudinem usitatae quasi familiaris peruersitatis uinculum abrumpere maiorum uirium est. et nequáquam desperandum adiuuante atque exhortante ipso domino deo nostro de gene [215] rosa libértate atque planñe uirili pectore tuo. incolumem te domini dei nostri misericordia tueatur, domine eximie meritoque honorabilis et dilectissime fili.

Date: Mid 402. Place: Hippo. Topic: Conflict regarding a clergyman named Timothy. and SANSUCIO and the brothers who are with us greet in the Lord SEVERO, most blessed and venerable lord, most beloved and true brother and priest, and those who accompany him.

1. We arrived at Subsana and found out what was done there against our will in our absence. We confirmed that some circumstances were as they had been told to us, while others had happened in a different way; but all were objects of pain and tolerance. With God's help, we correct them, partly with a rebuke, partly with a reprimand, and partly with prayer. What saddened us most, after the departure of your holiness, was that the brothers were allowed to leave without a guide for the journey. We ask that you forgive him and know that it was done more out of timidity than malice. Those here thought that our son Timothy had sent those brothers to anger your charity against us, and they wanted to leave everything as it was until our arrival, assuming that you would come with us. Therefore, God wanted to show the enemies of the Church, through your brother and our son Maximian, that there are within them those who do not seek their own interests, but those of Jesus Christ. Your brother did not abandon the ministry of the dispensation of the mysteries of God, overcome by some secular greed, but he deposed it moved by peaceful piety; He did not want, to save his honor, an ugly, threatening and perhaps disastrous schism to be generated among the members of Christ. Would there have been any conduct more blind and worthy of vilification than abandoning the schism of Donatus for the peace of the Catholic Church, to later disturb the same Catholic peace for a point of personal honor? As for your brother, let us celebrate having found him such that the storm of this trial has not destroyed what the divine word built in his heart. For the same reason we ask and beg God that, with his future life and his customs, he demonstrates more and more to the people how well he would have executed what he would have executed, undoubtedly, if it had been agreed.

To the blasphemous Porphyry, you fall into the snare of Hebion, when you said that Jews who believe in Christ must observe the law. Understanding that what you say is dangerous, you insist on tempering it again with superfluous words: "without considering them necessary for salvation, as some Jews considered them, and without celebrating them out of fallacious simulation, as Paul had rebuked Peter." 17. Peter therefore pretended to keep the law. On the other hand, Paul, Peter's rebuke, observed the rites boldly, since your letter continues: "If he celebrated those sacraments and pretended to be a Jew to win over the Jews, why did he not also sacrifice with the Gentiles, since he also acted as lawless with those who were outside the law, to impose it on them as well? No doubt he did the former because he was Jewish by birth. And he spoke thus, not falsely pretending that he was what he was not, but feeling in his mercy that he should help the Jews, as if he himself were in their error. That was not the cunning of a liar, but the work of a merciful man. You defend Pablo well. It turns out that he did not simulate the error of the Jews, but that he was truly in error. He did not want to imitate Peter, who dissembled and acted out of fear of the Jews, but he said quite freely that he was a Jew. Your clemency with the Apostle is great news! While trying to make the Jews Christians, he became a Jew. He could not reduce the spendthrifts to frugality if he did not demonstrate that

He was spendthrift, nor could he mercifully help the poor, as you write, if he did not feel miserable. Truly those are unfortunate and worthy of merciful pity who, through their desire to contend and their love for the abolished law, made the Apostle of Christ a Jew. There is no great difference between your sentence and mine, after all: I say that both Peter and Paul fulfilled the law out of fear of the Jews, or rather they simulated its fulfillment; You affirm that they executed the same thing out of mercy, "not with the cunning of one who lies, but with the affection of one who shows compassion." It seems, therefore, that they pretended to be what they were not, out of fear or mercy. And that other argument that you use against me even speaks in my favor, namely, that Paul should have become a Gentile for the Gentiles, as he became a Jew for the Jews; because, as he was not really a Jew, he was not really a Gentile either; and as he was not really a Gentile, so he was not really a Jew. But he became an imitator of the Gentiles, because he admitted the foreskin in the faith of Christ and allowed people to eat indifferently the foods that the Jews condemn, and not because of the worship of idols, as you think 8. Because, in Christ Jesus, neither circumcision nor the foreskin is anything, but the observance of the sacraments of God. 18. I beg you, then, and I ask you again and again to forgive this minor dispute of mine and to blame yourself for it.

very worthy and brothers worthy of just honor. 1. I am not surprised that Satan disturbs the spirit of the faithful. Resist him by maintaining hope in the promises of God, who cannot deceive. You distort things in vain. It is very clear who you are. The brothers who debated with you have updated me. You assure that you do not fear death \ That's fine. In any case you must fear the death that you cause to yourself by blaspheming God. You understand that this visible death that all men know consists of the separation between the soul and the body. You don't need great talent for this. But you add on your own that death is the separation between good and evil. If you think that the mind is good and the body is evil, surely the person who amalgamated them was not good. How do you say, then, that it was God who mixed them? From there it would be deduced that either God was evil or he feared evil, if that God that you pretend to be was so afraid that he mixed good with evil. holy and beloved brothers of God, justly venerable and desired.

1. When our dear brother Celso came to demand the letter from me, I hastened to settle my debt. Do not doubt my haste. While I thought he would stay with me for a few days, he suddenly found an opportunity to set sail, and at night he announced his intention to leave the next day. To do? He could not stop him, and even if he could, he should not, since he was going to you, with whom he finds himself more comfortable. That is why I hastened to dictate and deliver this little thing to you, confessing that I am indebted to a more prolix letter when I have been satisfied with the return of the venerable brothers Theasius and Evodius, my colleagues1. Because I hope, in the name and help of Christ, that in his heart and lips you will come more fully than in a letter. Tunacian, presbyter of the church of Tagaste, who is a soul with me and was leaving for Rome. So I ask you now what I usually ask, so that you do what you usually do: pray for me so that the Lord contemplates my humility and my work and forgives all my sins. 2. If you deign to accept my proposal, I want to discuss with you those points that we would discuss if we were together. You already solved my little doubt with Christian understanding and devotion. I proposed it to you a little while ago, as if we were exchanging some sweet words together. But you have been brief and too fast. The grace of your language could have stopped and expanded a little more on that point, glossing that same position that you have determinedly adopted and from which you deliciously benefit, according to your words, although, if God pleases otherwise, you remain willing to put God's will before your own. Because tell me: how can we know that will of God, which must take precedence over ours? Only when we willingly accept what we have to accept by force? In that case we execute what we do not want; We give our consent in response to the will of Him whose will and excellence we cannot reject and whose omnipotence we cannot resist. For example, another girded Peter and took him where he did not want; He went where he did not want, and yet he willingly submitted to a violent death. Or is it perhaps also when we can maintain our attitude in justice, but something happens that

shows us better the divine will and invites us to modify ours? In that case ours is good, and would continue to be so if God did not demand another from us. For example, Abraham did not do wrong when he raised and educated his son with the intention of continuing to do so until the end of his days as long as it was on his side; but suddenly he received orders to kill him and changed his attitude; and not because the previous attitude was bad, but because it would have started to be bad if it had not been modified when receiving the order. You certainly support my own opinion on this point. 3. But the usual thing is that we are forced to verify the difference between God's will and ours, not by a voice from heaven, nor by a prophet, nor by a revelation or dream, nor by that outburst of the mind that we call ecstasy, but by occasional circumstances that demand a change of plan. For example, we are determined to go on a trip and suddenly something happens; We consult the Truth about our obligation and she vetoes our journey. Or, on the contrary, we are determined to stay at home and suddenly an event is announced to us; We consult the Truth and it forces us to leave. Please explain to me more fully and precisely what you think about this third type of reasons we have for changing our will. It is common that in such circumstances we are disturbed; It is easy to skip something that should be done because we refuse to change our mind. True, our opinion was not bad, but it becomes bad by postponing what we occasionally have to do.

They laudably observed these observances in their time, as dispensers of the Gospel, so that the many weak Jews who had believed and continued to understand that the rites should not be proscribed would not be scandalized; On the other hand, he is crazy who now tries to observe them by simulation, once the doctrine of Christian grace is published in all nations and is confirmed in all the churches of Christ by the reading of the Law and the Prophets; In Scripture it is discovered that these observances must be understood, but they must not be observed. But in that case I can also affirm that the apostle Paul and the other Christians of right faith had to guarantee the ancient sacraments, observing them truthfully for some time, so that posterity would know that they should not detest as diabolical sacrilege the observances of prophetic significance kept by the most pious fathers. 17. I really confess that I expressed myself less well in what I put in my letter, namely: that Paul, being already an apostle of Christ, had accepted the celebration of the Jewish mysteries to show that they did not harm those who wanted to observe them, since they had received them from their fathers by the law. I should have warned: "only during the generation in which the first grace through faith was revealed." Because at that time that was not harmful. With the progress of time, those observances would be abandoned by all Christians, while, if they had then been abandoned, the distinction would not have appeared between what God commanded by the ministry of Moses and what the unclean spirit established in the temples of demons. Therefore, my negligence in not having added this explanation to you is more culpable than your rebuke. However, before receiving your letter I had clarified my thoughts, by writing against the Manichean Faustus, as your kindness will be able to see if he deigns to consult that place. I did not omit that clause there, although I explained it briefly. Those of our dearest friends for whom I am sending you this letter will also be able to read it, and you will be able to verify it as you wish. As for my thoughts, believe me, as I ask you with the right of charity speaking before God: I never supposed that the Jews converted to Christianity should now celebrate, with any motive or intention, those ancient sacraments, nor that it would be lawful for them to do so.
