The same Apostle also said: Behold, I, Paul, tell you that if you are circumcised, Christ will be of no use to you. If so, did he deceive Timothy and make Christ of no use to him? Perhaps because he did it fallaciously, the problem was avoided? He did not suggest that circumstance of the simulation. He did not say, "Whether you circumcise yourselves sincerely or falsely," but without exception He said, If you circumcise yourselves, Christ will profit you nothing. You want to make room for your opinion here and you want to imply "if you go around, unless you do it fallaciously." Well, in the same way I am not shameless if I ask you in that passage to let me understand that it was said: if you are circumcised, to those who wanted to be circumcised because they thought that otherwise they could not be saved in Christ. To those who at that time were circumcised with that spirit, with that will, with that intention, Christ did not

took advantage at all. This is what the Apostle says clearly in another place: For if righteousness is obtained through the law, Christ died in vain. That is said in the same passage that you cited: You who are justified in the law have been cut off from Christ; you detached yourself from grace. Then he attacks those who believed they were justified in the law, not those who observed such ceremonies in honor of the one who prescribed them; because these understood that the observances had been prescribed as an announcement of the Truth and also how long they should last. That is why he also said: If you are guided by the spirit, you are no longer under the law. Because it is well known, as you deduce, that he who is under the law lacks the Holy Spirit, whether he acts by dissimulation, as you say about our elders, or sincerely, as I understand. 20. I consider that it is a great problem to determine what it means to be under the law, as the Apostle says in a pejorative sense. I don't think he says it because of circumcision or because of those sacrifices that the fathers offered in their time and Christians do not offer now, or because of similar rites. Suffice it to say that the law also commands: You shall not covet, and we confess that Christians must also observe it. The evangelical illustration proclaims it very loudly. The Apostle says that the law is holy, and the command, holy, and just, and good. Furthermore, he adds: Has what is good then become death to me? Not such, but sin, in order to appear as such a sin, has gone away.

The same thing that he says here, that sin increases exceedingly because of the command, he says elsewhere: The law was established so that crime would abound. But where crime abounded, grace abounded all the more. And in another place, where he is speaking about the gift of grace, which justifies, he asks: What then can we say about the law? This question is answered below: It has been established for reasons of prevarication, until the lineage to whom the promise was made arrived. Therefore, the Apostle says that those whom the law makes criminals are punishably under the law, because they do not comply with it and boast of their own strength, with boastful pride, without understanding the office of grace, necessary to fulfill the precepts of God. Because the fullness of the law is charity. But the charity of God has spread in our hearts, not by ourselves, but by the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us. But to sufficiently explain this problem, a more extensive and exclusive treatise is perhaps required. When the law says you shall not covet, it exposes the criminal if human frailty is not helped by the grace of God. That law condemns the prevaricator, rather than saves the sinner. For how much less can he justify to anyone circumcision and similar rites, which were imposed for reasons of symbolism and figure, and which must necessarily have been abolished when the revelation of grace spread everywhere?

Date: Year 404/405. Location: Hippo. Topic: The inheritance of the monk Honorato. AUGUSTINE and the brothers who are with him greet ALIPIO, most blessed lord, venerable brother, dearest and much desired, and companion in the episcopate, and the brothers who accompany him. 1. The sadness of the church of Thiave does not let my heart rest until they tell me that those of that church have been reconciled to you in the ancient harmony. That has to be soon. The Apostle showed great interest in a single individual when he said: Let no one who did that let himself be dominated by sadness; and in the same place: So that Satan does not dominate us, since we are not ignorant of his intentions. How much greater vigilance will be necessary to demand so that we do not have to regret this in an entire flock, especially in the case of a flock that has just been added to the Catholic peace and which in no way can I abandon? Since the lack of time did not allow us to meet together to deliberate diligently to reach a clear conclusion, may your holiness receive what I have determined after we separated and after having matured it with rest. Bishop Rogato of Cartenna, in Ja Mauretania, converted to Catholicism and was persecuted by the Donatists. These had the help of Firmus, brother of the tyrant Gildon (Reply to the letters of Petiliano 2,3). In turn, Firmo was the son of Nubel, whom the Moors considered their king. This king was subject to Rome, but he helped the Donatists and persecuted, at their suggestion, the rogatistas, or supporters of Rogato. That is why the Donatists were called "Firmians." Date: Year 406/408. Location: Hippo. Theme: Protest against the cruelties of the circumceliones.

The CATHOLIC CLERGY of the region of Hippo to GENARO '. 1. Your clerics and circumcelions are attacking us in a persecution of a new type and unprecedented cruelty. Even if they returned evil for evil, they would still work against the law of Christ. But it is the case that, if we compare our actions with yours, it is discovered that we suffer what is written: They returned evils to me for good; and in another place: With those who hated peace I was peaceful; While I was talking to them, they fought me for no reason. Your age is already advanced. But we think that you know perfectly well that the party of Donatus, called in its beginnings in Carthage the party of Majorinus, without cause accused Caecilian, then bishop of the church of Carthage, before the then emperor Constantine. Maybe your gravity has forgotten it, or you hide that you know it, or maybe you ignore it, which we don't believe. So that this does not happen, we include in our letter a report from the then proconsul Anulinus, whom the party of MaLXXXVIII had questioned [CSEL 34/2,407]

Tell us, who forced your elders to use the proconsul to refer Caecilian's case to the emperor and to denounce to the emperor a bishop, whom you had already sentenced while he was absent? 6. So you have no reason to complain about us. However, the meekness of the Catholic Church lived completely peacefully, after those orders from the emperors when your clergy and the circumcelions, with their cruel infamies and furious violence, began to fight and destroy our tranquility. They forced us to remember and bring to light the ancient edicts. Before these new laws about which you currently complain were implemented in Africa, your people laid traps for our bishops on the roads, injured the clerics with very serious wounds, also inflicted cruel torments on the laity and set fire to their houses. A priest, because of his own free will he preferred to join our communion, was kidnapped from his house, brutally beaten at his whim, dragged to a muddy pond, dressed in reed fabric and, as a display of his feat, they showed him off, to some to mourn him and to others to laugh at him. In the end they took him wherever they wanted, and only after twelve days they released him 3. Our bishop reprimanded Proculeiano in the municipal minutes, and he dissembled, without making any inquiry. He again warned him urgently, and Proculeyan declared on record that he would not say another word. Those who carried out this feat are today your priests, and they still sow terror among us and persecute us as best they Can. 6.

We give them freedom without causing them any inconvenience, just as we detain them without causing any inconvenience when they refuse to adhere to the unity of Christ because of their excessive obstinacy, when we are ashamed to tolerate the insults of those who raised so many slanders against us and plotted so many atrocities against us, or also when we fear that they will suffer with us the injuries that they used to make us suffer. As far as we can, we advise this same conduct to our lay people, so that they retain them unharmed and bring them to us so that we can amend and instruct them. Some of our people listen to us and obey us, if they can; others, it is true, behave towards them as towards bandits, since in reality they are victims of bandits. Some avoid their own wounds with the sword and escape by wounding; Others imprison them, present them to the judges and, despite our intercession, refuse to forgive them, because they fear that the prisoners will later carry out revenge. But, in the meantime, the criminals do not renounce their behavior as bandits and demand the honors of martyrs. 10. They confess that baptism is legitimate and authentic when they baptize a criminal of their own, as long as their crimes are hidden. We ask them: "Who baptizes in that case?" Perhaps you will say that the wise must understand and interpret everything that ancient times wrote about the life and customs of the gods in a very different way. In fact, I have heard that for a short time here certain healthy interpretations have been read to the people gathered in the temples. But please, is the human race so blind and so enemy of the truth that it does not see things so clear and noticeable? Look at the number of places where Jupiter, in the act of committing his numerous adulteries, is painted, cast, beaten, sculpted, described, read, imitated on stage, in song and in dance. Does it seem too much to you that, even in the Capitol, it is read that he forbids such sins? Will it be said that cities flourish, when all these shameful and impious infamies boil among the people, without prohibition; when they worship each other in temples, they laugh in theaters; when victims are offered to them, while the flock of the poor lives in misery; when the actors imitate and represent them, while the patrimony of the potentates is ruined? I tell you this because you write to me that, the closer your life is to its end, the more you want to leave your country unscathed and flourishing. Suppress so many vacuities and follies, convert men to the true worship of God and chaste and pious customs, and then you will see your country flourishing, not in the opinion of fools, but in the truth of the wise. When this carnal country in which you were born becomes part of that country in which one is born by faith and not by the body, in which all the saints and faithful to God will flourish in an endless eternity, after the winter toils, so to speak, of this life, then you will see it. I have a truly cordial interest in not losing Christian meekness and in not leaving in this city for which you advocate an example whose imitation could be harmful to others. Otherwise, that meekness that I wish to maintain and that discipline that I zealously want to use moderately can be prevented, if this pleases God in His hidden judgments, if He judges that such an immense crime as has been committed should be punished with a severe scourge or if He manifests a more fearsome wrath, temporarily leaving those who do not correct themselves or convert to Him unpunished. 7. To measure this crime by the rigor of public law, it must be punished with more severe censure. «A bishop – you say – must only provide health to men, intervene in the causes to soften them and deserve forgiveness from the omnipotent God for the crimes of others. That is precisely what I want to do: that no one punishes with a more severe censure, neither me nor anyone else when I intercede. I desire to give men health, which consists in the ease of living righteously, and not in impunity for behaving iniquitously. I strive to deserve forgiveness, not only for my sins, but for those of others as well, although I cannot ask for it at all, except for those corrected. Another thing you add: "For this reason I make the most earnest plea, so that if this matter admits of defense, those who are not guilty are defended and the innocent are no longer bothered." 8. Listen for a moment to the terms of the case and yourself separate the guilty from the innocent. Contrary to the laws promulgated very recently 5, a sacrilegious solemnity, a pagan festival, was celebrated on June 1st, without anyone prohibiting it. And it was celebrated with such insolent audacity that not even in Julian's time was it done. The brazen mob of dancers even passed before the very doors of the church of that city. The clerics tried to prohibit such illicit and shameful insult, and then the church was stoned. Eight days later, the bishop once again demanded compliance with “quod quidem si iuris publici rigore metiamur, deben plecti seueriore censorship; sed episcopum", inquis, "fas non est nisi salutem hominibus impertiré et pro statu meliore causis adesse et apud omnípotentem deum ueniam aliorum mereri delictis." hoc omnino seruare conamur, ut seueriore censorship nenio plectatur ñeque a nobis ñeque ab alio ullo intercedentibus nobis, et salutem hominibus cupimus impertiré, quae posita est in recte uiuendi congratulate yourself, non in male faciendi securitate. ueniam quoque non tantum nostris uerum et aliorum instamus delictis mereri, quod impetrare nisi pro correctis omnino non possumus. adiungis etiam et dicis: "Quanta possum supplicatione deposco, ut, si defendenda res est, innoxius defendatur, ab ínnocentibus molesta separetur." 8.

The next day, our men wanted to draw up a record of what they thought was appropriate, with the aim of instilling fear in the guilty; but they were denied public rights. On that same day, as if God wanted to frighten them, a hailstorm fell as a response to the stones. At the end of the hailstorm, they completed the third stone throw, and, finally, they set fire to the buildings and the ecclesiastical men. They killed a servant of God who, as a fugitive, was able to confront them. Of the rest, some hid wherever they knew how, others fled wherever they could. Meanwhile, the bishop, constricted and shrunken, hid in a certain place, from which he heard the voices of those who were looking for him to kill him and who rebuked themselves because their great crime was useless since they did not find the bishop. All this was carried out almost from four in the afternoon until late at night. None of those whose authority could be weighty attempted to restrain the criminals; No one tried to help, but a stranger. Through this, many servants of God were delivered from the hands of those who were preparing to kill them. He stole many things from the savage looters.

9. Therefore, in that entire city they could not separate the innocent from the guilty, but, in any case, the guilty from the most guilty. Because only small is the sin of those who did not dare to provide help because they were especially terrified of offending those who had power in the city and were known as enemies of the Church. But criminals were all those who, if not by direct actions and management, at least by consent, cooperated in the perpetration of the crime. More criminals were those who committed it. And those who took the others were very criminal. Regarding the latter, let us assume that it is pure suspicion and not truth; Let us not discuss what we could only find out by subjecting those whom we should make sing to torment. Let us also grant permission to the fear of those who thought that praying to God for the bishop and for his servants was a better conduct than opposing the powerful enemies of the Church. Do you think that the rest should not be subjected to any discipline or that an example of such barbaric fury should be recommended with impunity? We do not try to feed our anger by asking for revenge for things past, but we are mercifully interested in thinking about the future. Christians have something to do with punishment, not only with meekness, but also with benefit and advantage, with respect to these perverts. These have the safety of the body to live, the means to live and even to live badly. Let us leave intact the body and the means necessary for them to live after repenting.

Date: Shortly before the year 408. Place: Hippo. Topic: The vision of God.

"Dre or couldn't he?" If we say that he could not do it, they proclaim that we suppress the omnipotence of God. And if we say that he could, then his argument and conclusion can be gleaned from our response. But the foolishness of those who affirm that the flesh will become the substance of God and become what God is is more tolerable; At least they make this flesh, which is not so dissimilar and diverse, suitable for seeing God. I believe that those we are now dealing with will throw out from their beliefs and perhaps from their ears this nonsense of the conversion of the flesh into the substance of God. And yet we can urge them with the same question: Can God or cannot God do such a thing? They will suppress divine omnipotence if they answer that it cannot, or they will confess that this will happen if they answer that God can. For in the same way that you would untangle yourself from another's bond, untangle yourselves from your own. Furthermore, why do they only try to attribute that privilege to the eyes of Christ and not also to the other senses? Will God then have to be sound in order to be perceived by the ears? And also breath so that it can be perceived by smell? And will it also be liquor so that it can be drunk? And will he have corpulence so that he can be touched? "No," they say. But how! Can God do that and not this? If they say He cannot, how dare they undermine God's omnipotence? If they answer that he can and does not want to, why do they favor only the eyes and despise the other senses of Christ? Do they perchance rave as far as they want?

Greet CIPRIANO in the Lord, most sincere lord, holy brother and co-presbyter.

I sent a letter to our blessed daughter Itálica, and I ask you to deign to deliver it to her. In it I said something against the opinion of those who can expect nothing from God, except what they perceive in their bodies. They do not dare to affirm that God is a body. But they indicate it in another way, by stating that it can be seen with the bodily eyes, that He created only to perceive bodies. I believe that these people do not know what a body is or how much of a spirit such as God is. Taking advantage of that opportunity with which I tried to console her, I did not want to overlook the place where the authentic consolation of this pilgrimage of all of us resides. Do not hesitate to tell me what they say against those who think otherwise, which I tried to briefly refute. Perhaps she is reluctant or ashamed to express that conflict, even if it is caused by someone else's presumption. Pay a little more attention to Cyprian's letter, so that you can see how inexcusable, according to him, is anyone who tries to separate themselves from the unity of the Church, which God promised and fulfilled in all nations. Such a person separates himself for the sake of his own righteousness. This way you will understand how much truth there is in the sentence that I mentioned above: The bad son declares himself righteous, but does not justify his departure. Cyprian, then, says in a letter that he wrote to Antonianus something decisive for the question at hand. But I'm better going to give you his own words: «Some of the bishops, our predecessors in this province, believed that peace should not be given to fornicators, and they completely closed the door to penance for adulteries. But they did not depart from the college of their co-episcopes nor did they break the unity of the Catholic Church with their obstinacy or censure. ,! Greet in the Lord PAULINO and TERASIA, most beloved and most sincere gentlemen, holy, desirable and venerable brothers and fellow disciples in the teaching of the Lord Jesus.

1. Our brothers, closely united to me, visit you frequently, and you are accustomed to paying them greeting for greeting and wish for wish. But that does not increase my goods as much as it consoles my evils. I strive to suppress the very cause and force of these evils that I do not love, but rather detest, for those who are forced to cross the sea, with all the zeal I can, and, despite that, I do not know how they can never be absent, surely due to the merit of my sins. Paul, Boniface's predecessor, had, upon being appointed bishop, the intention of renouncing all his property due to the immense amount of tax debts he had incurred. 1. I heard that you had been promoted for your merits. You want my humility to instruct you and that the Lord, by whose gift you are what you are, use your religious obedience to protect his Church. Date: Year 408? Location: Hippo. Topic: Original sin and baptism.
Greets in the Lord BONIFACIO', companion in the episcopate.

1. You ask me if parents harm their baptized children when they want to cure them through sacrifices made to demons. And if they do not harm them, why does the faith of their parents benefit the child in baptism, when their disbelief cannot harm them? I answer that the virtue of the sacrament, that is, of healthy baptism within the holy organization of the Body of Christ, is so great that when someone, who was begotten by carnal delight, has once been regenerated by the spiritual will of others, he can no longer be bound by bonds of other people's iniquity if he does not consent of his own free will. The soul of the father, says the Lord, is mine, and the soul of the son is mine. The soul that sins, she will die. It is clear that she does not sin when she does not know that her parents or anyone else celebrates sacrilege to demons. Guilt is not communicated by the will of another, as grace is communicated by the unity of the Holy Spirit. But, on the other hand, the spirit of man cannot belong to this man and that man, so that it can be the common guilt when this one does not sin and that one does. That is why he who answers that he is immolated now, when asked, does not lie. The sacraments would not be sacraments at all if they did not have certain similarities with those realities of which they are sacraments. Because of this similarity, they are usually named after the same realities. Just as in its own peculiar way the sacrament of the body of Christ is the body of Christ, and the sacrament of the blood of Christ is the blood of Christ, so the sacrament of faith is faith. Now, believing is nothing other than having faith. Therefore, when you answer what a child who does not yet feel the affection of faith believes, you answer that he has faith through the sacrament of faith and that he is converted to God through the sacrament of conversion, because that same answer belongs to the celebration of the sacrament. Thus, speaking of baptism itself, the Apostle says: We have been buried with Christ through baptism into death. It does not say: "We have begun to symbolize the burial," but: we have been buried. Then he gave the name of the same reality to the sacrament of such a great reality. 10. Note on the following letter ("Retract.",

1. «Meanwhile, six questions were sent to me from Carthage. A certain friend presented them to me, whom I wanted to make a Christian, so that he could solve them against the pagans, especially since some of them were proposed, as he said, by the philosopher Porphyry. But I do not believe that it is that Porphyry Siculus, whose fame is so famous. I collected the disputes on these six questions in a book, not long, whose title is: Six questions resolved against the pagans. The first deals with the resurrection; the second, from the time of the Christian religion; the third, of the distinction of sacrifices; the fourth, about that passage: With the measure that you measure, you will be measured; the fifth, of the Son of God according to Solomon; the sixth, of Jonah the prophet. 2.

In the second I said: the health of this religion, by which health is truly, truthfully and exclusively promised, never lacked anyone who was worthy; and if anyone was lacking, he was not worthy. I did not say it as if one were worthy by his merits, but in the style that the Apostle says: Not by works, but by him who called, it was said: "The older will serve the younger", affirming that this vocation belongs to the purpose of God. creation and by whose participation every rational soul is blessed. 12. Therefore, from the beginning of the human race, whoever believed in Him, whoever in any way understood Him and lived justly and piously according to His precepts, through Him were saved without a doubt, wherever and however they lived. As we now believe in Him, who currently resides in the Father and once came in mortal flesh, so did the ancients believe in Him while He resided in the Father and was to come in flesh. According to the variety of times, what was then announced as coming is announced now already accomplished, but that does not mean that faith is different or salvation is different. The same thing is preached or prophesied with different rites and sacraments, but that does not mean we have to understand that they are different things or different salvations. Let us leave it to the counsel of God to decide what is and when it is to be fulfilled that which belongs to an identical liberation of the faithful and just, and let us retain obedience. The signs and names of that time were different from those of today; Before they were more hidden, now they are clearer; Before few fulfilled them, now many; but it is one true religion that is meant and observed. 13. We do not object to them that Numa Pompilius imposed on the Romans a cult of the gods different from that previously observed in Italy; nor that in the times of Pythagoras a philosophy was imposed that anteriorsapientia, per quam creata est uniuersa natura et cuius participatione omnis rationalis anima fit beata. 12.

Stop, then, objecting to us what can be objected to every sect and every religion of any name. They confess that times do not rush by chance, but flow orderly by divine providence. If they affirm that the Pythagorean discipline did not always or everywhere exist, because Pythagoras was a man and could not achieve that much of its effectiveness, can they even affirm that, at the same time in which he lived and in the places where this philosophy prevailed, all those who could hear it believed it or spontaneously followed it? Even if Pythagoras had had enough power to preach his dogmas wherever and whenever he wanted, even if he had added to that power an extreme prescience of things, he would not have appeared in any time or place, but where and when he knew that men would believe him. QUESTION III The distinction of sacrifices 16. Let us now look at the question that follows: «Christians denounce the sacred rites, the victims, the incense and the rest that the temple maintained; but, at the same time, they (or the God whom they worship) initiated that same cult, when God is presented to us as in need of first fruits. 17. It is seen that to present this question they allude to that place in our Scriptures in which Cain offers God a gift of the fruits of the earth, and Abel of the firstfruits of the flock. To this it is answered that the passage serves to demonstrate how ancient a thing sacrifice is; The truthful and sacred letters do not allow it to be offered except exclusively to the true God. But not because God needs him, since in those same books it is clearly recorded: I said to the Lord: "You are my God, because you do not need my goods." God looked to the good of man both when he accepted and when he rejected or received those sacrifices. It is us who benefit from worshiping God, and not God himself. When He inspires us and teaches us how we should worship Him, He does so for our maximum usefulness and not because of any need of His. Such sacrifices are symbolic and express the similarity of some realities. Through these symbols we are admonished to scrutinize, know or remember those realities symbolized in them. One thing I will not overlook in this brevity, namely: the temple, the sacrifice, the priesthood and the other things that belong to this point, the false gods (that is, the demons, who are the prevaricating angels) would never have demanded of those worshipers whom they seduce, if they had not known that they were indebted to the true God. point that they seem to live and breathe; especially if you add the veneration of the crowds who offer such high worship. 19. This morbid and pestilential affection is cured by Holy Scripture by instilling in us something well known, but applying the healthy remedy of its admonition, when it tells us: They have eyes and do not see, they have ears and do not hear, and similar things. These words are a well-known and common truth, but they instill a healthier modesty in those who offer such simulacra a divine worship with trembling, in those who contemplate them with veneration and adoration, as similar to living beings; to those who offer their prayers as if they were present, who sacrifice victims to them, fulfill vows and feel so affected that they do not dare to believe that their idols are meaningless. And lest such people believe that our books mean only that such affections derive from idols to the human heart, it was clearly stated: Because all the gods of the Gentiles are demons. That is why apostolic discipline is not content with saying what is read in John: Brothers, beware of idols, but adds what is read in Paul: What then! Shall I say that something has been sacrificed to idols or that the idol is something? In no way, but what people sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God; and I do not want you to become partners with demons. From which it is seen that what the true religion rebukes uiuere ac spirare uideantur accesonte praesertim ueneratione multitudinis, qua tantus eis cultus inpenditur. 19.

In the superstitions of the Gentiles it is not immolation, since the ancient saints also sacrificed God, but the immolation of false gods and impious demons. The truth exhorts us to become partners with the holy angels. Likewise, ungodliness drives society with demons. For her the eternal fire is prepared, just as the eternal kingdom is prepared for the society of saints. 20. From what has been said, the wicked cannot deduce the defense of their sacrilege and simulations, because they interpret in elegant ways what they want to mean. Their entire interpretation is referred to the creature and not to the Creator, to whom only the servitude of religion is due, which in Greek is expressed with the sole name of A.atpeía. We do not say that the earth, the sea, the sky, the sun, the moon, the stars and some aerial powers that do not appear in sight are demons, but that the creature is partly corporeal and partly incorporeal which we also call spiritual. It is manifest that what we do piously and religiously comes from the will of the soul; that is the spiritual creature that must come before the corporeal one. Whence it follows that sacrifices are not to be offered to the corporeal creature. Only the spiritual remains, which can be pious or impious: it is pious in men and in just angels, who serve God; It is impious in wicked men and angels, whom we also call demons. They should not present and bring up a single fact, as if it alone were incredible, but all those that are equal or even more surprising. But suppose that what is said about Jonah were said about Apuleius of Madaura or Apollonius of Tyana, 6 to whom many prodigies are attributed without citing any faithful author; although I also confess that demons imitate the holy angels, performing similar wonders in appearance, although not in reality, with absolute fallacy, not with wisdom. If it were said that those whom they kindly call magicians or philosophers had performed such a feat, they would no longer burst with laughter, but with pride. Laugh, then, at our Scriptures; Laugh as much as you can, while each day you see yourself more diminished either by death or by conversions. Meanwhile, all those predictions that the prophets left us written continue to be fulfilled, not only for us to read, but for their successors to verify through experience. Those prophets would laugh long ago announcing that they would fight in vain against the truth, they would bark in vain, they would be left alone. 33. It is neither absurd nor importunate to ask what all this means. By exposing it, we will believe not only that it happened, but also that it was recorded to mean another reality. Whoever wants to study the reason for the fact must first admit

without hesitation that Jonah spent three days in the vast belly of a sea beast. It did not happen in vain, but it is true that it happened. For if we are encouraged to believe things that are only said allegorically and did not happen, how much more should we be encouraged by things that are not only said allegorically but also happened? As human custom uses words, so divine power also uses facts. And just as human language acquires a certain luster when new or less common words are interspersed with moderation and decency, so the divine power stands out more brilliantly in wonderful facts that contain some consistent meaning. 34. But why are we going to investigate the significance of the prophet being devoured by that beast and coming out alive on the third day, when Christ himself explains it to us? This evil and adulterous generation asks for a sign, and no other sign will be given to it than that of the prophet Jonah; As Jonah was in the belly of the whale three days and three nights, so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights. It is long to explain, and in other places it has been explained a thousand times, how those three days of the death of the Lord Christ are to be understood. Understanding the whole by the part, the first day and the last enter in, and thus form three days in total with their three nights. Jonah went from the ship to the belly of the whale; Thus Christ went from the cross to the tomb or the depths of death.

You have exposed, regarding the current lawsuit, the thoughts and votes of my heart. I am a man and I confess to ignoring what is hidden in the thought of God. But I am absolutely certain that whatever it is, it is undoubtedly the most just, the wisest, the most firmly founded with an incomparable excellence above all the judgments of men. Because what we read in our books is true: There are many thoughts in the heart of man, but the thought of God remains forever. God knows and we do not know what time will bring us, the facilities and difficulties that will arise before us, the decision, in short, that we can suddenly make in accordance with the correction or hope of correction that the current lawsuit brings us. We do not know if God will be outraged by these events in such a way as to punish the guilty more severely with the impunity they ask for; or if he will judge them mercifully with that other mode of repression that pleases me; or if, finally, his harshest correction will come, but healthier because it is spontaneous, and then God will withdraw the terror he was preparing and turn it into joy through a true conversion to his divine mercy and not to that of men. 23. Perhaps you dislike us because imperial orders force you to enter the unit. You were the cause. Your violence and terror have prevented us from preaching the truth everywhere so that anyone who wants could hear it and safely adopt it. Do not raise your voice or alter your spirits. Consider patiently, if possible, what we tell you. Remember the exploits of your circumcelions and the clerics who were always at their head, and thus you will understand what is the cause that has brought you to the current situation. You complain unfairly, since you forced all this to be imposed on you. In order not to repeat excessive and remote events, remember your recent behavior. Marcus, a priest of Casfaliano, became a Catholic by his own decision, without anyone forcing him. Yours have persecuted him; They would surely have killed him if the hand of God had not used some men who intervened and repressed the violence. Restituto de Victoriana went, without anyone forcing him, to the Católica. He was kidnapped from his home, beaten, rolled in the mud, dressed in a reed cloth and held for I don't know how many days in prison; Surely he would not have been released if Proculeiano had not seen the threat of having to appear before the authorities for this reason weighing on him. Marcian of Urga spontaneously chose Catholic unity. He fled, but your clerics beat his subdeacon until he was almost lifeless, covered him with stones and demolished both their houses for that crime. 4. What else will I tell you? Lately you have sent a crier to announce in Siniti: "Everyone who communes with Maximinus will have their house burned." As? Before Maximinus converted to Catholicism and when he had not yet returned from his voyage, we sent a priest to Siniti with the instructions that he should not bother anyone, visit our people and within his own house preach Catholic peace to those who wanted to. You threw him out of there with grave insult. When our Possidio, bishop of Calama, went to the Figuline countryside, he only intended to visit our people, even if they were few there, and convert those who wanted to listen to him to the unity of Christ. That's the only reason I was going to preach the word of God. Well then; When he was on his way, they laid traps for him in the style of bandits. He was able to free himself from their hands, but then they tried to burn him alive, with the house in which he had taken refuge in the Olivet countryside, with the most brazen violence. And they would have achieved it if the settlers of that field, due to the risk they themselves ran, had not put out the fire that had been lit for the third time. The heretic Crispin was convinced of this crime before the proconsular court, but through the intercession of the same bishop Possidius he was not forced to pay ten pounds of gold. Ungrateful for that benevolence and meekness, he dared to appeal to the Catholic emperors, provoking against you with his importunity and vehemence that wrath of God of which you complain so much. 4.

5. You see that you violently rebel against the peace of Christ and suffer for your iniquities and not for Him. What madness is it to carry out actions typical of bandits when you live badly, and to demand the glory of martyrs when you are punished with justice? In this way, by your private and violent audacity, you force men either to go into error or to remain in error. How much better should we make use of the justly established authorities, which God, in fulfillment of his prophecy, has subjected to the law of Christ, to resist your excesses, so that the unfortunate souls may be freed from your domination, so that they may emerge from their inveterate falsehood and take refuge in the patent truth? Regarding those of whom you say that we forced them against their will, there are many who want to feel obliged to free themselves from your oppression, as they confess to us before and after their conversion. 6. Tell me, is it not better to add true orders from emperors in favor of unity than to add false indulgences in favor of perversity? This is what you did, and in a short time you filled all of Africa with your lies. And with that you only demonstrated that Donato's party always presumes to lie. That is what you boast and that is what you propagate, as it is written: He who trusts in falsehoods feeds the winds. That indulgence is as true as were the crimes of Caecilian and the betrayal of Felix Aptungense, who was the one who ordered Caecilian, and as is clear5. Let your bishops gather a thousand councils and respond to that single sentence; then we will agree with you in what you like. See how much perversity and impiety there is in what you say: “If a man is good, he sanctifies the one whom he baptizes; while if it is evil, and the baptized person ignores it, then it is God who sanctifies. You also tell us: The oil of the sinner will not anoint my head. The answer is: "That was said of the soft and deceitful caress of the soft flatterer, because the heads of sinners are anointed and grow when they are praised in the desires of their soul and those who acted iniquitously are glorified." This is clear from the previous verse, which says: The righteous man will correct me with mercy and rebuke me, but the oil of the sinner will not anoint my head. Date: End of the year 409. Place: Hippo. Topic: Barbarian invasions.
Greet VICTORIANO in the Lord, most beloved sir, much desired brother and co-presbyter.

1. Your letter has filled my soul with immense pain. You ask me to give you some answers in a long-winded work, when more long-winded groans and lamentations are due to such misfortunes than long-winded books. Because the entire world is afflicted by so many catastrophes, that there is hardly any part of the earth where the evils you mention are not committed and lamented. Very recently, in those solitudes of Egypt, where the monasteries, away from all noise, seemed to be protected from all contingencies, the brothers were beheaded by the barbarians. I believe that you are not ignorant of the atrocities that are now being committed in Gaul and Italy. Similar news has already begun to arrive from the many regions of Spain, which for so long seemed exempt from such atrocities. But why go so far? And now CXI [CSEL 34/2,642]

Since the barbarians have not reached our region of Hippo, the thefts of the Donatist and Circumcelion clerics devastate the Church in such a way that the crimes of the barbarians are perhaps more tolerable. What barbarian could imagine, like these, pouring lime and vinegar into the eyes of our clerics, after mistreating the other members with horrendous sores and blows? They also loot the houses of some and set them on fire; They pluck their dry fruits, spill their liquids and, threatening others with similar revenge, force many to be rebaptized. One day before dictating this letter to you, they announced to me that in one place forty-eight souls were rebaptized under the influence of similar terrors. 2. These things should not cause us strangeness, but pain. We have to beg God to deliver us from so much affliction, not according to our merits, but according to his great mercy. For what should the human race expect, seeing all these things prophesied so long ago in the Prophets and in the Gospel? We should not contradict ourselves to the point of believing them when we read them and complaining when we feel they are fulfilled. On the contrary, those who were unbelievers when they read or heard such prophecies in the holy books, must at least now believe, when they see them being fulfilled. Thus, from these pressures, as if we were in the winepress of the Lord our God, the oil of the faithful who confess and pray must not cease to be squeezed and flow. Date: Year 409/410. Location: Hippo. Topic: Congratulations and exhortation to Catholic proselytism. Greet DONATO in the Lord, an excellent lord and honorable brother in the most sincere love.

1. When you came to Tibiris for administrative reasons, I could not see you, although I very much wanted to. But I believe that this happened so that I could enjoy your spirit much better, now free from public care. A meeting in which we had found ourselves, I too idle and you too busy, would not have sufficiently satisfied the desire in either of us. Many, or rather all, whom I have asked, or whom I have heard when they spontaneously praised you, praise and celebrate with absolute uniformity your continence and the courage of your administration. I have accepted everything without scruple, because there is no dissonant voice, and with greater certainty, because your panegyrists were unaware of our friendship and did not have the slightest suspicion that I knew you. So I can't imagine that they tried to flatter my ears instead of preaching true virtues about you. Because praise is very far from vanity when reproach is sure not to hurt. However, oh excellent and honorable brother with most sincere diligence! I do not have to teach you now, but perhaps to remind you that popular fame and glory are not satisfactory in the mouths of the vulgar, but in the reality of themselves. Your actions are precious, even if they displease the common people, due to their own weight and brilliance and not because of the acceptance of the inexperienced. He who rebukes such actions must be pitied more than he who is rebuked for them and considered unhappy. When they are good and are also popularly celebrated due to due acceptance, the judgment of others does not make them greater or better. Because it reaches full integrity due to its intimate truth and is consolidated with the power of consciousness alone. Date: Year 403/423. Location: Hippo. Topic: Plea for help on behalf of a certain Favencio.
Greet in the Lord CRESCONIO', most beloved sir and brother justly honorable and worthy of being welcomed.

I cannot dissemble in this cause about which I am writing to your eminence again. Not only you, but also the interested party for whose cause Favencio has been kidnapped, will accuse me and rightly reprimand me. This person would come to think that, if he resorts to the help of the Church in the event that something similar happens to him, I will equally inhibit his need and tribulation. Furthermore, although I disdain people's opinions, what will I say or what account will I give to God our Lord if I do not worry with all my strength for the health of the one who asked for favor and help from the Church, at whose service I am, most esteemed lord and venerable son? And, since it is incredible and almost impossible that you do not already know why Favencio has been arrested, I pray to your dignity that, in the meantime, you deign to support my request.

Date: After the previous one. Location: Hippo. Topic: Plea for help in favor of the aforementioned Favencio. AUGUSTINE greets FORTUNATO in the Lord, most blessed lord and most beloved brother with veneration and co-priest, and all those who accompany him. Your holiness knows Favencio well, who was a tenant farmer in the Paracian mountain range. Fearing I don't know why the lord of the estate, he took refuge in the church of Hippo. And there he was, as fugitives usually are, waiting for the matter to be resolved through my intercession. As often happens, his caution diminished with time, and he came to feel almost safe from the enemy's inhibition. But, while leaving dinner with a friend of his, he was suddenly kidnapped (by order of a certain Florentino, the governor's bailiff, they say) by a group of armed people, who seemed enough to carry out the kidnapping. They announced it to me, without knowing who had kidnapped him, although suspicions fell on that man for fear of whom he had sought protection in the Church. 11. You thought you should entangle me or rather overwhelm me suddenly with an innumerable multitude of questions, supposing me to be free and idle. But when could I solve, no matter how much flexibility I had, so many difficulties for a man who is in such a hurry and who is almost, as you write, with one foot on board? The sheer number of problems would prevent me from doing so, even if the difficulties were easy to solve. But it is the case that they are involved in so many perplexities that, even if they were few in number, they would tire my attention for a long time until I gnawed my nails 1 even if they found me idle. And you see what things are: I would like to take you out of the middle of your delicious studies and associate you with my care, so that you would learn not to be vainly curious or at least not dare impose the burden of feeding and nurturing your curiosity on a man whose greatest concern is perhaps to repress and restrain the curious. Only because of that misfortune have you stopped seeing the reason that could induce me to give you what you requested. You are dominated by the perverse concern of learning what you ask me for the sole reason of being praised or not being reviled by men. For those reasons that you allege you have thought, with the same perversity, that I would be inclined to answer. I wish I could immunize you against that vain and fallacious good of human praise, when I tell you that I have been inclined, not to give you what you ask for, as you say, but to correct you! "The customs of men, you say, are prone to reproach." And what do you conclude? "If someone does not know how to answer when asked, you add, he is reputed to be unlearned and foolish." Here I am going to ask you something, not about Cicero's books, whose meaning cannot perhaps be ascertained, but something about your letter itself and the meaning of its words. I want to know why you did not say: "Whoever does not answer will prove to be unlearned and foolish," but you preferred to say: "He will be considered unlearned and foolish." Surely you understand that this individual is not unlearned and foolish, but is considered such. But I warn you that whoever fears being pruned 2 by the tongues of such esteemers is a dry log, and, therefore, is not only considered unlearned and foolish, but truly is and proves to be so. 5. For you do not see the truth, nor can you see it in any way while you lift up falling joys on human tongues. 6. And if that is not the purpose of your conduct and your intention, would you not want to be considered unlearned and foolish for some other reason? And what reason is this? Perhaps you pretend that it is not so difficult for you to access temporal riches, achieve an advantageous marriage, win honors and similar things, which pass in a dizzying current and snatch those who fall into them into the abyss. Nor is it decorous for me to serve you to achieve that end. It is rather decorous for him to separate you from him. I do not forbid you to put your end in the contingency of fame so that you emigrate from Mincio to Po. The Mincio River would hinder you even if you did not want to emigrate. Indeed, the vanity of human praise will not satisfy your avid spirit, since it offers no other nourishment than emptiness and air. The same greed forces us to turn to another object that seems more nutritious and fruitful. But, if the new object also flows in the current of temporal expiration, it is like a river that leads to another river, so that misery does not end as long as the end of our duties is placed in an unstable end. I want you, then, to rest on some sure and immutable good the construction of your constant zeal and the most secure rest of all your good and honest activity. The Word God together with God was generated in a very different way, which no one can understand except the one whom God inspires. Who will not see that Anaximenes errs in the same bodies, when he says that the air is generated and makes it God, and, on the other hand, he does not call God who gives being to the air, since someone has to produce it? Not because Anaximenes adds that the air is always in motion will our man be disturbed or accept the divinity of the air, if he knows that all movement of the body is inferior to the movement of the soul and that the movement of the soul is much more clumsy than that of immutable and eternal Wisdom. 24. In the same way, suppose that Anaxagoras or anyone else calls the same truth and wisdom mind. What am I interested in discussing words with him? It is evident that the mind produces the form and manner of all things and that it is rightly called infinite, not because it occupies spaces and places, but because of its power, incomprehensible to human thought. But it does not follow that wisdom is formless. Only bodies would be formless if they lacked limits. Cicero, to refute, what seems to be adversaries

25. "Moreover, Cicero continues, if Anaxagoras presents the mind as a kind of animal, it will carry within it a soul that justifies that name of animal." In this way, the mind would be like a body and would have a soul within it to be able to receive the name of animal. Cicero adopts in his arguments the custom of the carnal, in accordance with the gross sense of those with whom he argues. At least, that's my opinion. If they had been able to wake up, Cicero would remind them that everything that thought perceives as a living body can be said to have a soul and that it is an animated being, but not that it is a soul. Cicero points out: "There will be something internally that justifies that name of animal"; and then he warns: "And what is more interior than the mind?" The mind cannot have a soul inside it to be an animal, since it is the most interior thing. Therefore it must have an exterior body, and it will be the interior, so that there is an animal. That is why he adds: "Put on, then, an external body." As if Anaxagoras had said that the mind cannot exist if it does not belong to some animal. If Cicero warned that this mind is the supreme Wisdom, which is not typical of any animal, because the truth is offered in common to all the souls that can enjoy it, look how urbanely he concludes: "That does not please them", that is, it does not please Anaxagoras that the mind he calls God is clothed with an external body in order to be animal. «Consequently, Cicero concludes, it seems that a pure and simple mind that lacks something escapes the power and knowledge of our understanding.

It is said that Democritus differed from Epicurus in cosmological questions, because Democritus believes that the concourse of atoms has a certain animal and vital force. He says, as I believe, that by this force the images themselves are endowed with divinity. Such images, to which he attributes divinity, are not those of all things, but those of the gods, and are the mental principle in all those beings to whom he attributes divinity. He calls them animated images, which usually benefit or harm us. On the other hand, Epicurus places nothing in the principles of beings, but atoms, that is, certain corpuscles so small that they can no longer be divided or felt by sight or touch. Epicurus states that through the casual concurrence of these atoms, the innumerable worlds, animals, souls and gods are formed. He gives them human form and places them, not in the world, but outside the world and between the worlds. He doesn't want to admit anything at all outside of the bodies. It surprises me that Democritus has not realized that his thesis is false, if for no other reason than this: if our soul is corporeal, as he wants, it is very small, since it is enclosed in a small body; and then it is impossible for the enormous images that come to touch the soul in all its parts. of the body, since innumerable images flow from said body, they respond that they flow and pass with such speed that in the continuity and succession of all of them a single one is seen and perceived. Cicero refutes this vanity by denying that an eternal god like that of said philosophers can be thought of, since it is made up of innumerable images that flow and pass. They say that the forms of the gods are eternal, thanks to the innumerable succession of atoms, because these corpuscles emerge from the divine body, so that others and others follow one another, and by that same succession they do not allow that nature to dissolve. "In that case, says Cicero, everything would be eternal," because there is no being that lacks that innumerable relay of new atoms that ceaselessly replace the perpetual flight of those that leave. On the other hand, "how will this god not fear death, since he is shaken without any intermission, he is agitated by the everlasting incursion of atoms?" For Cicero, every wounded body is shaken by the atoms that burst in; He says that what is penetrated is agitated. Furthermore, "since images are always coming out of that body," about which we have already said enough, how can you trust in its immortality?,5 31. But there is something more regrettable in the delusions of those who hold such an opinion. The mere relationship of such delusions should be enough to reject them without opposition or discussion from anyone; and yet the keen wit of men took it upon themselves to refute them copiously, when even the most clumsy had to

laugh and get away from them. Because, even if you grant that there are atoms, even if you grant that they push and shake each other by chance collision, why should you simply grant that those atoms, which clash by chance, form any being, in such a way that they modify it by form, determine it by figure, beautify it by equality, illustrate it by color and animate it by soul? Whoever likes to look rather with the mind than with the eyes and asks for light from Him who made being, sees that all this cannot be accomplished except through the intervention of the art of divine Providence. In no way could even the existence of atoms be granted. I will omit the subtleties that the learned teach about bodies, but you can see how easily the falsehood of that theory is proven by the very opinion of its defenders. They claim that everything in nature is either body or void, or properties of both. In this last paragraph, I think they allude to movement, collision and the consequent forms. Tell, then, into what class you place the images, which, according to this opinion, flow from the most solid bodies; They are not solid, because they cannot be felt except by the touch of the eyes, when we see, and by the touch of the mind, when we think; and such organs are bodies. They judge that the aforementioned images come from the bodies and come to the eyes and the soul, which, according to them, is also corporeal. I ask if images also emerge from atoms. If they sprout, how can indivisible atoms exist?

Date: Year 410. Place: Unknown. Topic: The trinity before reason. CONSENT to AUGUSTINE,
holy lord and most blessed father.

1. I had already suggested in a few words to your holy brother and bishop Alypius, whom I admire with all the strength of my soul, the subject of my request, hoping that he would deign to support my prayers before you. But since the need to go to the farm has cut off the possibility of meeting you, I have preferred to send you my request by letter, rather than continue in the same uncertainty of mind. Above all, taking into account that the solitude of the place where you are will contribute, in my opinion, to refining your understanding, which penetrates the highest mysteries, if you see that you can grant me what I ask of you. To somehow define my personal position, I believe that it is necessary to perceive the truth of divine things by faith rather than by reason. Because, if the faith of the holy Church had to be perceived by reasons and discussions, no one would achieve beatitude except philosophers and orators. And so it pleased God, who chose the weak of this world to confuse the strong and save believers CXIX [CSEL 34/2,698]

Date: Shortly after the previous one. Location: Hippo. Topic: Response to the previous one. AUGUSTINE greets CONSENCIO in the Lord, a most beloved brother and worthy of honor in the womb of Christ. 11. Faithful piety respects only totally true reason. That is why we do not hesitate to dispel a certain idolatry that the weakness of human understanding tries to establish in our hearts through the habit of thinking about visible things. We do not dare to affirm that this invisible, incorporeal and immutable Trinity whom we worship is like three living masses, as large and beautiful as you want, but cut out by their own limits and reciprocally united to each other in their places. It does not matter that we place one of them between the other two, so that it separates them and they are each attached to one of their sides, or that we suppose that the three touch each other in the shape of a triangle, so that none of them is separated from the other two. 20. We must avoid thinking that God is similar to our justice since the light that illuminates is incomparably more excellent than the one who is illuminated. For how much more must we flee from believing that God is something inferior and, so to speak, more colorless than our justice? And what else is the justice that is in us, or any other virtue that makes us live uprightly and wisely, but the beauty of the inner man? And truly we were made in the image of God according to this beauty, rather than according to the body. That is why we are told: Do not be content with this world, but be reformed according to the newness of your mind, so that you may prove what the will of God is, what is good and right and perfect. We speak of the mind without referring to any corpulence or parts arranged in their corresponding locations, as when we see or imagine bodies; We allude to an intelligible virtue, which is justice, and we know it and believe it beautiful, and, according to that beauty, we are reformed into the image of God. For much less should we suspect that the beauty of God, who formed us and reforms us in his image, must consist in any corpulence. We must believe that it is as incomparably more beautiful than the mind of the just, as it is incomparably more just. Enough of these warnings that I present to your attention, perhaps somewhat more verbose than you expected if we stick to the custom of epistolary style, but brief if we look at the importance of such a high issue. I didn't do it to satisfy your eru20.

As if the one God, Creator of all things, who wants all men to be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth, had not been able to acquire both peoples and had possessed one instead of the other! And what does beloved by reason of parents mean? How or where does being dearly loved come to you if you do not believe and persist in being enemies of God? Thus it was said: I hated those who hated you, Lord, and I was consumed by your enemies; with perfect hatred he hated them. I think that it is the father's voice that says to the Son, through the prophet, in that same psalm, as he had previously said about believers: My friends are highly honored, God; His principality has been greatly strengthened. What does it profit them for salvation, which is only obtained through the faith and grace of Christ, if they are very dear to God because of their parents? What good does it do them to be loved, since they must be condemned, since, disagreeing because of their infidelity in the faith of the prophets and patriarchs, their relatives, are enemies of the Gospel of Christ?

You should not, therefore, diminish your works of mercy, but should expand them more than you used to. [ 1 ] Correspondence with Nebridius.—Critics believe that Augustine himself published this small collection (Lietzmann), either as a tribute to his friend, now as philosophical notes, or as an example of a frustrated vocation in Nebridius. It seems to us that Augustine's interest and motivation were deep. For his own part, it meant the process that followed his conversion, the spiritual retreat, the change of mentality and Christian progress, compared to his friend, who remained stagnant. From a random and skeptical situation he has reached stability and security in the meaning of his life, although one could speak of a "lost future" (P. Brown). On Nebridio's part, Agustín feels a mixture of affection and sadness that can serve as an example for his monastic institution. Nebridius, a taster of problems, but immature and stagnant in his aporetics, was Augustine's favorite disciple. He followed him to Rome and then to Milan, always harassing him with his witticisms and witticisms. When Augustine and Alypius were converted, he stood on the sidelines, unable to accept a stable and existential commitment. He considered Casiciaco's retreat as vita philosophica and, despite the friendship, he was not baptized at that time. When the friends returned to Africa, he followed them, but staying halfway on a farm he owned near Carthage with his own family. He estimated that the Augustinian foundation of Tagaste must correspond to a Platonopolis, and he hoped that Augustine would continue eternally telling him suggestive things about Plotinus, Plato and Christ. Little by little we see how the two friends are distancing themselves. Nebridius realizes that Augustine has changed direction, giving himself over to Christian caritas, and protests. His protest no longer has meaning or value, since Agustín, on the contrary, tries to attract his friend towards the religious vocation, delicately inviting him to come to Tagaste. There is no longer agreement between the vita philosophica and the vita religious. On the other hand, a painful theme arises for Augustine: it is Nebridius's mother who stops her son and stands between him and Christ, and Augustine will never forget that theme (cf. Letter 243). Then an illness occurs, which does not seem to be a sufficient reason to abandon the religious vocation. But suddenly death occurs (year 388-9), and the correspondence is cut off. Probably around then the death of Adeodatos, Augustine's son, also occurred.

He remains silent, but later we see that those deaths had left a deep wound in his heart. We think, therefore, that this correspondence with Nebridius was for Augustine a frequently repeated case in the monastic environment, as confirmed in The Sermon of the Lord on the Mount and in the Letter to Léto. Its publication is due to its instructive character. [2] Donatism. Segundo appointed an interim intervener, who was murdered in the church; and 5) Ceciliano was accused of guilt. Second, as if Carthage were his own seat, he assembled the council of his bishops, inviting Caecilian to attend. He, knowing the intrigue, did not attend. As was known, Ceciliano is condemned. The Carthaginian clergy, who had elected Caecilian, joined the Numidians. Once the consecration of Cecilian was annulled, Mayorinus, one of the servants of the Spanish Lucilla, was consecrated as archbishop of Carthage. The council sends communications to Rome, Spain, Gaul and the African provinces. Once all this was done, the Numidian bishops returned to their seats, triumphant. But the following year (313) Mayorino died and was succeeded by Donato de Casas Negras, who gave its name to Donatism. And since Caecilian does not give in, two antagonistic ecclesiastical parties appear, whose respective tendencies are not yet completely clear. In October 313, Pope Miltiades accuses Donatus of having "rebaptized" some traditor clerics and of constituting a "schism." On April 15, the Donatists presented two writings against Caecilian to the proconsul Anulinus, so that he could send them to the Emperor Constantine. That was putting the cause in the hands of the emperor. Constantine orders Anulinus to send Caecilian to Rome, with ten bishops from each faction, and passes the cause to Pope Miltiades. This, with the advice of some bishops of Gaul, condemns Donatus and vindicates the innocence of Caecilian. The Donatists challenge the sentence and appeal again to the emperor, alleging that they had not been given the offered Gallic bishops, but rather Italian ones, and that their African council was more numerous, consisting of seventy bishops. The following year (314) Constantine moved the court to Arles. But here too they condemn the Donatists and formally prohibit the rebaptism of traditors.

Donatus knew how to take advantage of the situation to provoke the hatred of the Africans towards Rome. As one of the objections was suspicion against Felix of Apthungi, one of Caecilian's "consecrators", Constantine commissioned an investigation. Felix is ​​declared innocent (year 315). Constantine, harassed by the Donatists and bored, accepts the review of the case, and in the fall of 316 finally declares that Caecilian is free from all suspicion and his opponents are simple "slanderers." In the spring of the following year (317), the repression of the Donatists begins. Their churches are to be confiscated. But Donatus, who had managed to flee from Italy to Africa, in Numidia resists handing over the churches to civil power and wins over popular opinion. Caecilian has to resort to military help to execute the imperial law. In this way, the division between two parties that accuse each other is already deepened and extended. The Donatists have the popular advantage. Catholics have the advantage of Rome. Causes of the Donatist phenomenon.—Many causes, remote and close, contributed to originating and characterizing the Donatist movement:

1) Rome's war against Carthage and the destruction of the Punic capital. 2) The colonization of the African province based on landowners and looking to the interests of Rome. 3) The "Punic" agricultural population, with its traditions, language and religiosity. 4) Controversy over the rebaptism of lapsary apostates between Saint Cyprian and Pope Stephen. 5) The imperial persecutions, which were considered oppression and inflamed a "religion of martyrs and heroes." 6) In the persecution there are many "traditors", Christians who, in the face of threats, deliver the Holy Scriptures, chalices, censers, ecclesiastical documents or lists of leaders to the civil authority. Although it seems that Donatism arose without sufficient reason, all these causes constituted an environment in which a simple spark (such as, for example, the suspicion of the "Numidians" towards Romanized cities, especially Carthage) was enough to cause a fire.

Character of Donatism.—It was undoubtedly an essentially religious phenomenon. As in any religious phenomenon, there are sociological and economic aspects, and of all lineages, but basically it is about "two churches" or "two altars", which raise the problem of the one Church of Christ. Is there Ecclesia? The Church was an "ark of salvation and purity" for believers in a corrupt world. Baptism was, therefore, the door to salvation. The Church was a Church of saints, and theoretically a Church without spot or wrinkle. Fundamentally, while Donatism opposed the "world", to preserve itself from it, Catholicism aspired to conquer the "world", as an inheritance from Christ. Some modern authors have tried to see the Donatist phenomenon as a socio-economic phenomenon, rather than as a religious phenomenon (FREND, W. H. C, The Donatist Church, Oxford 1952), but they contradict themselves from the very title. They deal with a "Donatist church" and not a "Donatist revolution" and they speak of bishops, clerics, councils, nuns, "soldiers of Christ", etc.: the people do not appear, unless led by clerical leaders, and there is no proletariat, but landowners (mainly Romans) who fight with the treasury and the imperial administration. The rebaptization.—It was providential for Augustine to have begun his controversy at this point, because in this way the central problem was revealed to him: «The Gentiles are the inheritance of Christ, and all the nations are the possession of Christ (Letter 23,3). Without denying any of the other aspects of Donatism, such aspects were like masks that hid its true face, and that is why the saint says: "Let us get rid of those useless aspects" (Letter 23,6). For him, Christianity must be identified with the "true religion", unique for the whole world (Letter 23,2; 43,8,21). The Donatists had not invented "rebaptism", since they had learned it from Saint Cyprian, and he had the greatest authority for them. But there was a notable difference. Saint Cyprian affirmed that, since the "unworthy" (heretics and schismatics) do not possess the Holy Spirit, they cannot transmit it. On the other hand, the Donatists placed "sinners" among the "unworthy", and thus a traditor, who delivered the Scriptures, was an infidel, since his sin was equivalent to the loss of faith. This then led them to other extremes, which forced Augustine to delve deeper into the doctrinal issue. How can a Donatist schismatic

validly administer baptism, even if it is for their own harm? How can you give what you don't have? And if that baptism is valid, why is it fruitless and harmful? The immediate response could consist of distinguishing between the sacramentum and the res sacramenti, between the rite and the grace; but the difficulty was to find biblical texts that clarify this doctrine. For this reason, Augustine is forced to rely on the authority of the Church, on Tradition, to demonstrate that the baptism of heretics is valid. So you have to go deeper. Thus, for example, when quoting 1 Cor 1:13 ("You were baptized in the name of Christ..."), he remembers the "law of levirate" in the O.T.: the one who engenders in baptism is the Church itself, even if it uses a schismatic or Catholic minister. Or put another way, Christ engenders in the Church, whether Catholic or schismatic. We must then distinguish four categories of baptized: 1) faithful Catholics, represented in Isaac and Jacob; 2) baptized by schismatics, but converted to Catholicism and represented by Asher: he was the son of a slave, but was added to the "People" by fraternal harmony; 3) baptized by schismatics who maintain "fraternal discord", and are represented in Ishmael and Esau; 4) finally, the baptized Catholics, but alienated by sin, will not possess the kingdom of God. Ecdesia omnes per baptismum parit, siue apud se, ex uterus suo siue extra se de semine uiri sui; siue de se, siue de ancilla (Baptism I 15,23: PL 43,121s). And each case demanded an appropriate explanation. For example, the belonging of these "sinners" to the Church created a difficulty for Augustine: they do not have grace or the Holy Spirit, and yet they live in charity and unity: this means that there is an objective charity and unity in the Church, which incorporates them into the hierarchical Church.
