Relationship with Saint Augustine 391.—When Augustine arrives in Africa, he begins to worry about the situation in the country. He meets Aurelio, deacon of Carthage and other Catholic leaders, and notes the defects of the situation. Suddenly Aurelius is elected primate of Carthage, and Augustine rushes to execute what he had in mind. 1) This is a religious problem and not a socio-economic one. 2) It is necessary to accept the Bible as the only criterion to solve this problem. Authority and faith rest on the Bible, not on bishops. 3) It is necessary to convene a council every year, to properly organize theoretical and practical behavior, 4) A "seminar" is opened in Hippo, to select and train bishops and leaders. 5) Double tactics against the schismatics: meeting and direct controversy with the leaders and bishops; direct information to the people about the history and situation and religious meaning of the schism. 6) Reform of the Church through preaching and action. 7) Charity and meekness of Catholics. Already in the first years some friends of Augustine, monks and seminarians of Hippo, were consecrated: 394.—Alipius, bishop of Tagaste. 395.—Augustine himself, bishop of Hippo. 397.—Severo, bishop of Milevi. 400.—Profuturo and then Fortunato in his place. 400.—Posidius, bishop of Calama. [3] Correspondence with Paulinus of Ñola.—This correspondence does not appear among the manuscripts of the letters of Saint Paulinus of Ñola, but among those of Saint Augustine, which indicates that they were collected and published in Africa, probably by Augustine himself, and that they occupy the years 394-417. Perhaps this collection was also intended to promote monasticism with the extraordinary example of Paulinus. Alypius began the correspondence, noting that he had already heard of Paulinus in Italy and had read one of his poems. But it is evident that Alypius is trying to establish a bridge between Paulinus and Augustine, and in fact, once that bridge is established, he remains silent. Paulinus' conversion to asceticism was a sign of the times, which were changing rapidly in those years.

But for Augustine it had the greatest importance, since it was difficult to believe that a senator would abandon his privileged Roman situation and distribute his assets among the poor. And since, around Saint Paulinus, other senatorial figures gave the same testimony of a change in historical mentality, Augustine tried to take advantage of that edifying example for his monks and for those who could hear those stories. On the other hand, Paulinus' letters were read and reread by Augustine

for his own edification. Some biblical texts and some allusions by Paulinus undoubtedly influenced Augustine's monastic mentality, since Paulinus collected testimonies and influences from other Italian friends. Especially if we take into account the influence of Saint Ambrose on Paulinus. Such happens, for example, with the theology of Pentecost. It is in Paulinus that we find for the first time the recourse to anima una et cor unum in Deum. Augustine took up the indication, expanded and deepened it, resorting to the original biblical text (Acts 4:32). A few years later, the two saints are concerned about the difficulty of knowing God's will in everyday casuistry. For Agustín this correspondence also has practical interests. It serves him to recommend his friends Romanianus and Licentius, to request copies of books, such as the Ecclesiastical History, by Eusebius, or a "History against the pagans", which Augustine has heard has been written by Paulinus, and of interest to Augustine in view of the events of the pagan reactions against the Christians, etc. Given the personality of Paulinus and the respect that Augustine feels for him, the rhetorical and refined nature of the formulas of friendship between the two saints is not surprising. [4] Correspondence with Saint Jerome.—The need to acquire Christian books moved Augustine to communicate with the East, and especially with Saint Jerome. In the year 393, Alypius traveled to Bethlehem and met Saint Jerome, no doubt commissioned by Augustine. Upon his return, Alypius was consecrated bishop of Tagaste, so that Augustine's first letter to Jerome dates from the year 394, or at most 395, since Augustine was still a priest (Letter 71,1,2). Profuturo, the new traveler, who was to carry the letter, was suddenly consecrated bishop and then died; The letter did not reach its destination, and was instead copied by others. The issues that worried Augustine were two: 1) Considering that the official authority of the Bible resided in the translation of the Septuagint, he believed that a direct translation from Hebrew (such as the one attempted by Jerome) would take away authority from the Greek, and that is why he disapproved of it. 2) Jerome interpreted the text of Gal 2, l l s as if it were an agreed simulation, and Augustine considered this to be a true lie. He made a separate study (De mendacio) to be able to oppose Jerome with confidence.

The letter, delayed and copied in Rome, reached Jerome through another channel, and in addition the term "lie" had to sound excessively harsh to him. Some friends of Jerome suggested to him the suspicion that Augustine wanted to embolden himself and become famous at the expense of the old fighter, and this hurt the monk of Bethlehem. Agustín wrote his letter again, and for the third time to request the answer, thus forcing the old lion to come out of his reserve. In this way, a correspondence and a discussion of the greatest interest were established, both for the points of view of both parties and for the character of both fighters and, finally, for the substance of the problem, the separation between Christianity and Judaism in the early times and today, a permanent problem in the Church. The three problems demanded his method, his position and his solution, and apparently on all three points Jerome had to recognize that Augustine was right. For this reason, once the first period of correspondence was over, Jerome understood the height and competence of Augustine in his defense of the Christian ideal and apologetic struggle, since Augustine perfectly distinguished between an "eristic", in the face of dogmatizing enemies, a "missionary theology" in front of those open to sincere discussion, and a "dogma-

ethics" itself, founded on revelation, for which a special study on revelation was required, without agreed upon "simulations" or reasons of state. Both doctors highlighted the drama of the Apostles Peter and Paul, when answering the questions of the catechumens of the early Church: "Why have we changed so much?" [5] Compelle intrate.—The fight against Donatism was not a personal problem. Agustín achieved personal successes to the extent possible, but he found himself framed in a legal, political, sociological and counter-revolutionary system that could not be avoided. In this way, Augustine was forced to accept the surrounding realities, beyond his personal idealisms and his religious ideals. Once Emperor Constantine had condemned the Donatists, the enemy arose against the emperors and against the Roman Empire. In this way, the movement took on a civil character, to which the civil authorities responded with the repression typical of those times. The legislation against heretics and schismatics that came from the imperial court and was very harsh, in Africa took on another, more offensive repressive character, for the aforementioned reasons. And the problem was complicated, since both Augustine and his friends were educated in Roman culture and many had been business managers or secret police, and they got along well with the officials of the Empire, while the Donatist leaders usually came from rural backgrounds and lived from a primitive fanaticism, which they did not even dare to confess with a clear conscience. All this forced Augustine to rethink the means of "converting" the Donatists, as he explains to us in Letter 93. The problem of terrorism is very delicate and complex. First of all, it is necessary to verify the fact of terrorism, and on this point Augustine could not doubt the violence of the circumcelions, protected by Donatism in general, despite many lamentations, as usually happens. Secondly, it is important to know whether the imperial laws of that time were adequate or exaggerated. Augustine could not intervene in them except indirectly. Once the problem is posed well, three positions immediately emerge. Those who exercise or defend terrorism will always reject the anti-terrorist laws that repress them.

That of those who suffer from this terrorism, who sometimes ask for greater rigor, sometimes are more humane and sometimes take meekness to the extreme: thus, for example, Augustine excludes the death penalty, the requisition of necessary goods and is content with superfluous goods and strictly personal defense. Finally, that of the indifferent. As Augustine himself raises the problem, it is very difficult not to agree with him and consider his position as soft and human. Asking for greater impunity would be excessive. On the other hand, the evangelical formula compelle intrare (force them to enter), could perhaps justify their changes in position.
